docs.title: Home
docs.text:
SlingologyEIS reads the engine logs your Garmin avionics already record on every flight and answers two questions about each one:

  1. Did anything go outside the Rotax Operators Manual limits?
  2. Was this flight unusual for your engine?

The limits come from Rotax. The idea of "usual" comes from your own flight history. What to do about either is your call — the app never silences anything on its own, and it never stops watching something you've told it to tolerate.

Open SlingologyEIS — it runs entirely in your browser. There is nothing to install and no account; the analysis happens on your computer and the results stay there. Your logs stay in your own folders — the app reads them; it never copies or uploads them. If you would rather run it as a program on your own machine, you can (how).

Keep a copy of your workspace

Your workspaces are kept by your browser, on this device. Clearing the site's data removes them, and a browser short of space may clear them on its own. Settings → App → Export workspace… writes one file that restores everything — make one after your first analysis and whenever you have made decisions you would not want to redo. How.

No logs yet? Try the sample workspace

Download the sample workspace (10 MB) — a season of N117ZS, the Sling TSi the app was developed on: 19 flights, the three filters its owner set and why, and one annotation. Open the app, go to Settings → App → Import workspace… and pick the zip; the app analyses the flights in about a minute. Then look at Trends for the widening EGT spread, open the 2 September flight to see the fuel-pressure filter at work, and read the Journal. The sample is the same workspace the screenshots on this site were taken from.

Every flight in a workspace, with its insights at a glance.

docs.title: SlingologyEIS
docs.text: Engine health analytics for Rotax iS aircraft engines — built for how a FADEC engine actually works.

docs.title: Two ways to read this site
docs.text:
If you want to get going, start with the walkthroughs. They are picture-led and take you from opening the app to making your first decision about an insight:

  • Open the app and your first workspace
  • Reading your first flight
  • From an insight to a decision
  • Export and import

If you want to understand what the app is telling you, read the concept pages in order. Each one opens with a short In brief that tells you what the idea is and where you meet it in the app; the rest of the page explains how it works and which settings shape it. Stop whenever you have what you need.

  • Understanding your engine's data — what EIS tells you, why a FADEC engine is different, logs, flights and workspaces, phases of flight
  • What EIS watches — limits and events, your reference, topics and insights, the topics, cylinder balance
  • Deciding what matters — your decisions, Trends, the Journal
  • Working with others — sharing a workspace

docs.title: Found a problem? Have an idea?
docs.text: Tell us on the SlingologyEIS feedback board — no GitHub account needed. In the app, the speech-bubble icon in the top bar opens it from any page. Report something that looks wrong, suggest a feature, or vote for the ideas other pilots have posted; the votes help decide what gets built next. When reporting a problem, say which page you were on, what you expected, what you saw and which browser you use, plus the This build line from Settings → App → About; a screenshot helps. If the problem is in the analysis of a flight, a workspace export lets it be seen exactly as you see it — say in the report that you can share one.

docs.title: What this app is, and isn't
docs.text: SlingologyEIS is a reading aid for the data your engine already produces. It will show you when a reading went past a limit, when a flight looks different from your own history, and when something about your engine has been slowly changing. It will not tell you whether your aircraft is airworthy, and it does not replace the Operators Manual, your maintenance schedule or your mechanic. When the app says something is worth raising with your mechanic, that is what it means — a conversation starter with the evidence attached, not a diagnosis.

docs.title: Which engines
docs.text: Rotax 912iS, 915iS and 916iS. The Operators Manual limits for all three are built in and verified against the manuals. The analytics themselves were developed and validated on a 916iS; on the other engines each topic is marked unverified until there is data from such an aircraft. See The topics for the status of each.

docs.title: Which logs
docs.text:
Four kinds of Garmin engine log: a G3X log copied from the SD card, a Garmin Pilot export of a G3X log, a Garmin AXIS log copied from its SD card, and the aircraft log the AXIS hands to Garmin Pilot, downloaded from flyGarmin. The app recognises the format from the file itself, a workspace can mix them, and the same flight found in two of them is shown once. More on logs.

Free and open source under the MIT licence. The project, its source code and the research paper behind the analytics are at github.com/AlchemyGeek/Rotax9iSEIS.

docs.title: Building the documentation site
docs.text:
The pilot documentation lives in this folder and is built with MkDocs and the Material theme.

pip install "mkdocs-material==9.7.*"
python3 docs/tools/gen_om_limits.py     # regenerate reference/om-limits.md from engines/*.json
mkdocs serve                             # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build --strict                    # static site into site/
mkdocs gh-deploy                         # publish to GitHub Pages

Layout:

  • concepts/ — one page per concept; In brief on top, how it works below, specs and paper as further reading
  • walkthroughs/ — picture-led, task-shaped pages
  • reference/ — limits (generated), settings, glossary, further reading
  • diagrams/ — hand-drawn SVGs inlined into concept pages (they follow the site's light/dark theme)
  • img/ — screenshots taken from the N117ZS workspace; retake as a batch after a UI change
  • specs/ and the research paper are kept here for developers and excluded from the site nav

docs.title: Theme override
docs.text: docs/overrides/partials/header.html is a copy of Material's header partial (from the version pinned in these instructions) with one addition: the Open the app button, which reads its address from extra.app_url in mkdocs.yml. After upgrading mkdocs-material, re-copy the partial from the new version and re-apply that block, or the header may miss newer theme changes.

docs.title: The Claude Desktop extension — developer note
docs.text: How the extension bundle (Spec 16 §7) is built, what it runs and how to work on it. The user's side is the walkthrough Install the extension.

docs.title: What the bundle is
docs.text:
An MCP Bundle (.mcpb, a zip with manifest.json at its root), one per macOS architecture: slingology-eis-<version>-macos-arm64.mcpb and …-macos-x86_64.mcpb.

Part What manifest.json manifest_version 0.3; server.type binary — the command is the bundled Python, so Claude Desktop needs no runtime of its own python/ A standalone CPython 3.12 (python-build-standalone, release and checksum pinned in scripts/build_extension.py) with the engine wheel and its investigations extra installed (numpy, pandas, scipy, matplotlib, pypdf). The wheel carries the built UI. icon.png The 512 px app icon

About 100 MB packed, 280 MB unpacked. No bytecode ships: the first start writes it into the extension's folder (about 9 s), later starts take a fraction of a second.

docs.title: What Claude Desktop runs
docs.text:
${__dirname}/python/bin/python3 -I -m slingology_eis.investigations.extension \
    --data-root ${user_config.data_root} --aircraft ${user_config.aircraft} \
    --log-folders ${user_config.log_folders}

slingology_eis/investigations/extension.py turns that into slingology-eis mcp serve --serve --port 8420 --log-file [--aircraft …] [--log-folder …]:

  • One process: the MCP server on stdio, and the EIS pages on http://127.0.0.1:8420/ on a thread. Desktop starts it and stops it (closing stdin ends it). If the port is taken — slingology-eis serve is already running — the pages aren't served from this process and the tools carry on.
  • User configuration (all optional): the data folder (empty → the one the pages use, Spec 02 §5.8.1), the aircraft (empty → the only one, else the most recently opened, D10), log folders (linked to the workspace the tools open once it exists; added, never removed). An unset setting arrives empty or as the literal placeholder; both mean not set.
  • Logs: Claude Desktop's own MCP logs (~/Library/Logs/Claude/, one file per server, named after it) and cache/mcp.log under the data root (started afresh past 2 MB).

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
cd web && npm ci && npm run build && npm run build:browser && cd ..   # UI → web/dist, wheel in web/dist/engine/
python scripts/build_extension.py --wheel web/dist/engine/slingology_eis-*.whl --out dist-ext

It must run on the architecture it targets (pip picks the running Python's wheels for numpy, scipy…). It downloads the standalone Python once into ~/.cache/slingology-eis (--cache to change), installs the wheel, prunes what isn't needed at run time (the test suite, IDLE, Tk), replaces symlinks with copies, checks the bundled engine imports with its UI, then validates and packs with npx @anthropic-ai/mcpb (pinned). CI does the same on macos-15 (arm64) and macos-15-intel (x86_64) after the main job, keeps the bundles as artifacts and attaches them to the release on a v* tag.

docs.title: Trying a build without installing it
docs.text:
mkdir /tmp/eis-ext && cd /tmp/eis-ext && unzip -q …/slingology-eis-*-macos-arm64.mcpb
python/bin/python3 -I -m slingology_eis.investigations.extension \
    --data-root /path/to/a/copy --aircraft "" --port 8432 --log-folders

then type MCP requests on stdin ({"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{}}), or open http://127.0.0.1:8432/. Always point it at a copy of a data root. tests/unit/test_extension.py covers the entry, the folder linking, the log file, the busy port and the manifest.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text: Not yet signed. mcpb sign signs a bundle with a PEM certificate and key, and mcpb info shows a bundle's signature status. Claude Desktop warns before it installs an unsigned bundle; the walkthrough tells the user what to expect. Signing with a CA-issued certificate is a later step.

docs.title: Starting the app
docs.text: SlingologyEIS runs in two ways. Both show the same screens and keep the same kind of workspace, and an export from one opens in the other.

docs.title: In your browser, from the website
docs.text:
1. Open https://alchemygeek.github.io/Rotax9iSEIS/app/ in Chrome or Safari on a Mac.
  2. The first visit downloads the analysis engine — about 30 MB, once. The page shows its progress.
  3. Create a workspace, then Choose folder… and pick the folder that holds your engine logs (or drop log files on the page). Sync analyses them.

Good to know:

  • Your logs stay on your computer. The engine runs inside the browser; nothing is uploaded. Workspaces are kept in the browser's private storage for this site.
  • It works offline after the first visit. Open the same address with no network and the app starts from your computer. When a new version is published, the next visit with a network switches to it and says Updated to version … once.
  • Safari asks for the folder again each visit. The folder shows Not connected — reconnect; pick it again, then Sync. Chrome remembers the folder and may ask you to Allow access with one click.
  • Keep a backup. The browser can clear a site's storage (for example when you clear browsing data). Settings → App → Export all workspaces… saves everything in one file you can import again.

docs.title: On your computer, as a local app
docs.text:
1. Install Python 3.10 or newer.
  2. Download the slingology_eis-….whl file from the latest release on GitHub and install it:
pip install slingology_eis-*.whl
  1. Start it, and open the address it prints (normally http://127.0.0.1:8420/):
slingology-eis serve

Your workspaces are kept in a SlingologyEIS folder in your home folder. Settings → App → Data location can move it. Add log folders by path; the app reads them where they are.

Stop the app with Ctrl-C in the terminal window.

docs.title: Publishing the website
docs.text:
Every push builds the site; CI keeps it as the artifact slingology-eis (slingology-eis-site.zip), and a release tag attaches it to the release. The site is plain files: it works from any folder of any static host, with no special server settings.

GitHub Pages serves this repository from the gh-pages branch, which the documentation already uses (mkdocs gh-deploy, at https://alchemygeek.github.io/Rotax9iSEIS/). The app goes in the app/ folder of the same site:

rm -rf docs/app && mkdir -p docs/app
unzip slingology-eis-site.zip -d docs/app      # from the release, or a CI run's artifact
mkdocs gh-deploy                               # publishes the docs with the app under app/

docs/app/ is not committed. Each publish adds the app's ~30 MB to the gh-pages branch history.

A custom domain is optional: set it in the repository's Settings → Pages. The app needs no change for it — the address in the first section changes, nothing else.

docs.title: Tagging a release
docs.text:
1. Set the version in pyproject.toml and slingology_eis/__init__.py (kept equal), and update CHANGELOG.md.
  2. Commit, then tag and push:
git tag v1.2.3
git push origin v1.2.3
  1. CI builds the tag, creates the GitHub release if there isn't one yet, and attaches the wheel and the site zip to it. Edit the release notes on GitHub if you want more than "See CHANGELOG.md."
  2. Publish the website from that release's site zip, as above.

docs.title: Cylinder balance
docs.text: In brief. On a FADEC engine the four cylinders should behave as a matched set, so the most telling single picture of engine health is how their cruise exhaust temperatures sit relative to one another — and whether that picture is changing. The app watches it two ways: the spread from hottest to coolest, and each cylinder's deviation from the other three. On Trends they are drawn together as one Cylinder balance panel: four lines that, on a healthy engine, run roughly flat and parallel.

docs.title: Why EGT pattern, not EGT level
docs.text:
The exhaust gas temperature of one cylinder on one flight depends on power, altitude, outside air and the day. The pattern across the four cylinders depends on the cylinders. Because the engine computer gives each cylinder the fuel and spark it intends, a cylinder that drifts away from its neighbours is telling you about an injector, a plug, an ignition coil or the probe itself — not about how the engine was leaned, because it wasn't.

Most engines have a cylinder that always runs hottest. On a turbocharged 915iS or 916iS it is usually cylinder 4, nearest the turbo exhaust. That is normal, and the app learns which cylinder is your usual hottest rather than assuming a flat ideal.

docs.title: Two measurements
docs.text:
Spread — hottest cruise EGT minus coolest — is the one-number summary, and the one the Operators Manual limits (392 °F between cylinders at normal fuel flow). The app compares each flight's spread with your usual spread in similar outside air temperature and watches for a widening trend over engine hours.

Deviation — each cylinder's cruise EGT minus the average of the other three — is the diagnostic version. It tells you which cylinder moved and in which direction. A cylinder running hotter than its own usual can mean a lean injector; cooler can point to ignition or a plug; erratic can point to the probe. The four deviations always sum to zero, so when one cylinder moves, the others appear to move the other way; the app reports the cylinder whose change is largest.

When one cylinder explains a widening spread, you get one insight under Cylinder EGT deviation, not two.

 engine hours °F vs others 0 Cyl 4 Cyl 3 Cyl 2 Cyl 1 usual pattern: flat, parallel · Cyl 4 hottest (turbo exhaust) Cyl 4 drifting away from the others → worth a look the four lines always sum to zero: when one moves up, the others appear to move down Healthy: four flat, parallel lines. Worth a look: one line drifting away.

docs.title: On the Flight view
docs.text: Two cards. Cylinder balance (EGT spread) gives this flight's spread, your usual, and the OM limit. Cylinder EGT deviation lists all four: Cyl 1 −33 °F (avg −32), Cyl 2 −18 °F (avg −9), Cyl 3 −4 °F (avg −7), Cyl 4 +55 °F (avg +48) — each cylinder against its own history. Both measure cruise only, so a flight without a settled cruise shows unavailable.

docs.title: On Trends
docs.text:
The Cylinder balance panel combines everything:

  • Four deviation lines over engine hours, with the reference band of whichever cylinder you select shaded behind them.
  • A hottest-cylinder strip: one mark per flight, shaped and coloured by which cylinder was hottest; hollow when its lead was under 15 °F (too close to call), ringed when it differed from your usual.
  • Usual hottest in the header — Cyl 4 (100 %, 57 flights, learned) — once one cylinder has won at least 70 % of ten or more flights by a clear margin. Until then the engine's expected cylinder is shown as a prior.
  • The spread strip below, with the OM limit drawn on it.

In the change summary at the top of Trends, the four deviations collapse to a single row naming the cylinder that moved most — cylinder 4 is about 6 °F running hotter than it used to (relative to the other cylinders) — and the spread ranks separately.

Trends → Cylinder balance: four deviation lines, the hottest-cylinder strip, and the spread.

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text:
• Four flat, parallel lines with the same cylinder hottest flight after flight: a healthy, consistent engine.
  • One line stepping or drifting away, especially if the hottest cylinder changes: look at that cylinder — injector, plug, coil, probe.
  • All four lines moving together cannot happen (they sum to zero); if the spread widens with no single cylinder responsible, the change is spread across cylinders and worth watching over more flights.
  • A noisy line on one cylinder with the others steady: probe or connector first.

As always, one flight is a note; a trend across flights is a conversation with your mechanic.

Further reading: Spec 08 (cylinder balance) and research paper §7.2 in the repository.

docs.title: Operators Manual limits and events
docs.text: In brief. The Rotax Operators Manual sets limits — temperatures, pressures, RPM, boost, time at takeoff power. When a reading crosses one for long enough to matter, the app records an event: when, in which phase, for how long and by how much. The engine computer's own ENGINE ECU alert is treated the same way, once the app has sorted the expected occurrences (start, lane check, shutdown) from the unexpected. Events are listed in the Events table on the Flight view and summarised on the Operators Manual limits card; a flight with any carries a LIMIT badge.

docs.title: Where the limits come from
docs.text:
Each workspace is tied to one engine model, and its limits come from that model's Operators Manual — the edition and revision are shown under Settings → Engine alongside the full table. The table is read-only: the limits are Rotax's, not the app's and not yours. What you control is what to do about an event that keeps happening (see Your decisions).

Twenty-one limits are checked on a 916iS, including per-cylinder EGT maximums, the EGT split between cylinders, manifold pressure, fuel pressure both ways, bus voltage both ways, and the five-minute rule for takeoff power. The 915iS and 912iS tables differ in a few values and in what exists at all — the 912iS has no turbo and no EGT-split limit. Operators Manual limits by engine lists them side by side.

Settings → Engine: every limit, its value, its severity label and when it is checked.

docs.title: How an event is found
docs.text:
A reading past a limit for a single second is not an event. Three rules keep the Events table honest:

Some limits need the excursion to last. Idle minimum must persist 30 s before it counts — a brief dip as the governor settles is normal. Fuel pressure minimum needs 10 s. Fuel pressure maximum needs 10 s in climb and descent but 30 s in cruise, where switching tanks causes a longer, harmless spike.

Some limits are only checked when they make sense. Low oil pressure, low fuel pressure and low voltage are not checked with the engine stopped. Oil pressure minimum is checked only once airborne. The oil-temperature-before-takeoff minimum is checked from the takeoff roll on. Fuel pressure maximum is not checked during taxi at all, because that is when you run the pump test. The Suppression column in the limits table shows these rules per limit.

Nearby excursions are one event. Once a reading has gone past a limit, the event does not end until the reading has been back inside for 30 s. A value that bounces across the line for two minutes is one two-minute event, not forty tiny ones.

What remains is listed in the Events table: time, phase, which limit, duration, how far past, and a link that jumps the chart to that moment — a triangle where the event started and a dashed line where it reached its worst value. Each limit appears at most once per flight.

The Events table: one row per limit exceeded, with phase, duration and excess.

docs.title: Severity labels
docs.text: Each limit carries a label from the manual's own wording — WARNING or CAUTION — and each event inherits it. The labels are there to help you read the table. The app does not treat the two differently: it does not hide a caution, escalate a warning, or decide on your behalf that one deserves action and the other does not.

docs.title: Time at takeoff power
docs.text:
The manual allows takeoff power — above 5,500 rpm, or 100 % power — for no more than five minutes at a stretch. The app measures the longest continuous block you spent there (with the same 30 s rule joining brief dips). Going past 300 s is an event like any other. Coming within a minute of it is noted on the Time at takeoff power card as a close call, which usually means power was not reduced promptly after takeoff — a long climb-out, a delay — and is worth a glance at your habits rather than your engine.

The 5,800 rpm ceiling is separate: it is a hard limit with no time allowance. A brief overshoot as the governor catches a prop is the most common cause, and the kind of thing a filter with a small tolerance is for.

docs.title: Engine computer alerts
docs.text:
The engine computer raises an ENGINE ECU caution on the panel for many reasons, most of them routine. The app records every occurrence and sorts it by what the aircraft was doing:

When it happened What the app makes of it While the avionics and engine computer were coming up, before or during start Expected. Counted on the Engine computer alerts in flight card, nothing more. During the lane check — stationary, RPM in the lane-check band, two short runs Expected; this is the single-lane test. The flight header reports both lanes ✓, one lane only or not detected. At shutdown, as the engine is cut Expected. Counted only. On the ground with the engine running, but not a lane check An event. Listed in the Events table with the reason it is not a lane check — for instance that the RPM was below the lane-check band. In flight, from the takeoff roll to the landing roll An event, and the one that matters. Not expected; worth having the engine computer's fault log read at the next maintenance.

Occurrences shorter than a few seconds are counted as blips and not treated as events, because a single logged reading can be an artefact. The lane-check band depends on the engine — around 4,000 rpm on the 916iS and 912iS, around 2,500 rpm on the 915iS.

docs.title: Where events go next
docs.text:
Events are facts about one flight, but their pattern over many flights is what tells you about the engine. Every limit that has ever been exceeded in a workspace gets its own panel on the Trends page, showing on which flights it fired and by how much. And a limit that fires on every flight for a reason you understand — a sensor that reads a little high, an installation quirk — can be given a filter with a note, after which the app shows those events collapsed into one line and keeps watching for the day the pattern changes.

Further reading: Spec 01 (engine contract) §§ on limit detection and CAS classification, and Spec 09 (limit filters), in the repository.

docs.title: Logs, flights and workspaces
docs.text: In brief. A log is a file your avionics wrote. A flight is a log the app has decided actually left the ground. A workspace is the app's view of one aircraft: the folders its logs live in, plus everything the app has learned and every decision you have made. Your logs stay where they are — the app only reads them — and you can have as many workspaces as you like, one active at a time. You meet all three on the Flights page.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Your Garmin avionics record an engine log every time the system is powered up. The app reads four forms of it, and the Flights page names each in its Source column:

Source Where it comes from G3X A G3X log copied straight from the SD card, named like log_20261005_172050_KAWO.csv. Garmin Pilot Garmin Pilot's export of a G3X log — usually a long random file name. AXIS card A Garmin AXIS log copied from its SD card. Aircraft log The log the AXIS hands to Garmin Pilot, which uploads it to flyGarmin; downloaded from there as aircraft-log-<tail number>-<date and time>.csv.

You do not need to tell the app which is which; it recognises the format from the file. A workspace can mix all four, and if you swap a G3X for an AXIS, your engine-hours history carries straight on, because both record the same engine meter.

Two things worth knowing about the aircraft log. It is the most complete of the AXIS's two records — it always starts when the avionics power up, so it holds the engine start and shutdown, and it carries the most reliable clock and the throttle position. And it carries no tail number inside the file: the app reads the tail number from the file name, so keep the name flyGarmin gives it. A renamed aircraft log still loads, but the app will ask which aircraft it belongs to.

The app never copies, moves, renames or edits a log. It reads the file, remembers what it found, and keeps a fingerprint of the content so that if you rename or reorganise your folders later, Sync recognises the same log in its new place.

A fresh workspace: add the folder your logs live in, or drop files onto the page.

docs.title: Flights
docs.text:
Not every log is a flight. The avionics log an engine run with the aircraft never leaving the ground, a three-minute circuit, a session where the system was restarted halfway through. The app sorts these out when it first sees each log, and lists the ones it set aside under Skipped on the Flights page, each with its reason:

Reason What it means Ground session The aircraft never got airborne — an engine run, taxi or run-up only. Short flight Airborne for less than 10 minutes. Meant to catch pattern work too short to say anything about the engine; a twelve-minute hop still counts. Corrupt log A gap of more than five minutes inside one log, usually an avionics restart or an SD-card hiccup. Unreadable Not a Garmin engine log the app can read, or a file it could not analyse. The reason is shown; other logs are unaffected.

The same flight often reaches you twice, and the app recognises it as one flight and shows it once:

  • A G3X log and its Garmin Pilot export are the same data; the app uses the more complete file.
  • An AXIS card log and the aircraft log of the same flight are two different recordings; the app keeps both and analyses the aircraft log. The Source column shows the analysed one first and the other as also: AXIS card. It does not matter which arrives first: your notes and decisions stay attached to the flight when the second one turns up.

If you think the app got one wrong, open it: a skipped log opens read-only in a Log preview with its chart and alerts, and Include this log overrides the decision and analyses it. Nothing is ever deleted.

Skipped logs stay listed with their reason, and can be included.

docs.title: Workspaces
docs.text:
A workspace is where the app keeps everything it derives from your logs — each flight's analysis, your reference, the decisions you have made, your Journal. It is tied to one engine model, chosen when you create it, because the Operators Manual limits differ between the 912iS, 915iS and 916iS.

A workspace is defined by one or more log folders. Subfolders are included. Add the folder where you already keep your logs (Choose folder…, or drop files onto the page) and the app reads whatever is there; add logs to that folder and the next Sync picks them up. A single log that has gone missing keeps its results until you choose to remove it.

Because the app runs in your browser, it reads your folders only with the browser's permission. Chrome keeps that permission between visits and occasionally asks you to confirm it (Allow access on the folder row). Safari forgets it when you leave, so the row shows Not connected — reconnect on your next visit; everything already analysed is still there, and you reconnect only to sync new logs or open a flight's charts. When the app runs as a program on your own computer instead, folders are typed as paths and stay connected; if one is on a disk that is unplugged, the app says so and offers Locate folder when it is back.

You can have as many workspaces as you like, and switch between them from the name in the top bar. Two reasons to have more than one:

  • Another aircraft. Everything the app learns about "usual" is learned from one engine and never applied to another, so a second aircraft needs its own workspace. If logs from two tail numbers end up in one workspace the app notices and says so on every page where it matters.
  • An experiment. A workspace that points at a folder holding only some of your logs — one season, one engine-hours range — gives you the same analysis on just those flights. The app does not filter flights for you; you choose by organising files in folders.

The workspace name is yours. The one you were last using reopens when you start the app.

docs.title: Sync and re-analysis
docs.text: Sync rescans the workspace's folders, finds new and moved logs, and asks before analysing: Found N new logs. Analyze now? It also tells you when existing flights need re-analysis — after an update to the analysis itself, or after you change something that affects every flight, such as assigning a log channel. Say yes once and the Flights page shows per-flight progress.

docs.title: Where things are stored
docs.text:
What Where Your logs Wherever you keep them. Never copied or modified. (Logs that arrived inside an imported workspace are the one exception: the app keeps its own copy of those, with that workspace.) Workspaces and their results In your browser's private storage for the site — on this device, in this browser. Settings → App → Storage shows the space used and whether the browser has agreed to keep it; Delete all data there empties it. It survives restarts and app updates, but not clearing the site's data, so keep a workspace export as your backup. Derived from your logs; safe to delete and rebuild. …when you run the app on your own computer A data folder (~/SlingologyEIS by default, shown and changeable under Settings → App → Data location). Back it up like any other folder.

A workspace belongs to the browser it was made in. To use it in another browser or on another computer, export it there and import it here — the export carries every decision you made, and the logs if you ask.

Walkthrough: Open the app and your first workspace.

docs.title: Phases of flight
docs.text: In brief. The app splits every flight into phases — pre-start, engine start, warm-up, taxi, takeoff roll, climb, cruise, descent, approach, landing roll, shutdown — from the RPM, airspeed and altitude in the log, with nothing for you to label. Almost everything else depends on this: cylinder balance is measured in cruise, boost on the takeoff roll, and a reading that is expected to be out of range during the pump test or at shutdown is only known to be expected because the app knows the phase. You see the phases as coloured bands on the Flight view timeline.

docs.title: Why phases come first
docs.text:
Engine readings only mean something in context. 47 psi of fuel pressure is above the manual's maximum, and on a long cruise that is worth knowing; during the fuel-pump test on the taxiway it is what the test is for. 0 volts at the end of a log is the master switch going off, not an electrical failure. EGT spread during the climb says little; during a settled cruise it says a lot.

Without phase awareness the fuel-pressure maximum "fired" on four flights out of five and the low-voltage limit on half of them, which is the fastest way to teach a pilot to ignore every alert. So the first thing the app does with a log is work out, second by second, what the aircraft was doing.

 pre-start start warm-up taxi takeoff roll climb cruise descent approach landing shutdown time → Oil and coolant peaks · time at takeoff power · OM limits (phase-aware) Cylinder balance · cylinder deviation · cruise fuel facts Turbo boost at takeoff fuel pump test — fuel pressure max not checked lane check (ENGINE ECU expected) Which parts of a flight feed which topics.

docs.title: The phases
docs.text:
Phase What the app is seeing Pre start Avionics on, engine not running. Engine start RPM coming up from zero. Warm-up Engine running, aircraft stationary. Taxi Moving on the ground. A run-up that drops back to idle without leaving the ground stays in taxi. Takeoff roll High RPM, still below flying speed and close to the ground. Climb Flying and gaining height steadily. Cruise Flying with the altitude held for long enough to settle — about a minute. Descent Losing height steadily. Approach Low and slowing, near the end of the flight. Landing roll Back on the ground, slowing, RPM low. Shutdown Engine stopping.

Everything is read from the log's own channels — RPM, indicated airspeed, altitude, vertical speed — after a little smoothing so that a single noisy reading cannot flip a phase. Field elevation is taken from the altitude while stationary before takeoff, and re-read wherever the aircraft next touches down, so a flight that lands at a higher airfield than it left still ends correctly.

The caption under the timeline chart lists how long the flight spent in each phase: taxi 6m 0s · takeoff roll 14s · climb 1m 51s · cruise 7m 20s … Hover the chart and the phase at the cursor is named.

Phases as coloured bands under the traces, with their durations listed below.

docs.title: What uses which phase
docs.text:
• Cylinder balance and cylinder EGT deviation use cruise only, where the engine is settled and the four cylinders can be compared fairly.
  • Turbo boost at takeoff uses the takeoff roll, at full power.
  • Time at takeoff power counts every second above the takeoff-power threshold, whatever the phase.
  • Oil and coolant peaks look at the whole flight.
  • Several Operators Manual limits are checked only in certain phases — oil pressure minimum only once airborne, oil temperature before takeoff only from the takeoff roll on, fuel pressure maximum not at all during taxi (the pump test) and only after a longer excursion in cruise (tank switching). The full list, limit by limit, is under Settings → Engine.
  • Engine computer (ENGINE ECU) alerts are sorted by phase into expected (at start, during the lane check, at shutdown) and not expected (on the ground with the engine running, or in flight). See Operators Manual limits and events.

docs.title: When there is no cruise
docs.text: A short flight, a pattern session or a flight that never settled may have no cruise at all. The cruise-based cards then say unavailable: no cruise detected rather than reporting a number from a few seconds of level flight, and the chart carries a note that phase detection did not find a clear climb or cruise. The flight still counts for everything that does not need cruise.

docs.title: Settings that shape this
docs.text: There are none to adjust. Phase detection is deliberately automatic; it uses the same rules on every flight and every aircraft so that flights stay comparable.

docs.title: From a finding to action
docs.text: In brief. A finding changes nothing by itself. It leaves Research when you take it somewhere: into the Journal, as a dated record; to the person who can act on it, as the notebook exported as a page; or to another owner, as a notebook they run on their flights. What you then do — fly differently, call someone, change a part, nothing — is a decision between you, the Operators Manual and the people who built the parts.

docs.title: Three ways out
docs.text:
The Journal. Ask Claude to note the finding in the Journal when it finishes — the one entry Claude may write there. It becomes one line under Research findings: the notebook's title and the finding in one sentence — the first line of its What the data shows — with the date and a link to the notebook. The Journal is the record of what you decided and why; a finding that led to a call, a change or a deliberate decision to do nothing belongs there. Then mark your question Watch or Acted, with a note, in the inbox.

A page for the person who can act. Export as a page (.html) on the notebook gives one file anyone can open, laid out like the notebook: the answer and the proposed actions first, then each finding with its numbered table, figure or log view, every number beside its reference. A proposed action already names who would do it and what it would settle; the one addressed to the manufacturer is where your message starts. In the oscillation case the propeller controller's manufacturer recognised a known behaviour from one email with a plot and the per-takeoff table, and offered a firmware update the same day.

Another owner. Export the notebook (.zip); another owner of the same engine imports it and runs it on their flights (Notebooks you keep and share). Two aircraft showing the same shape is a different conversation with a manufacturer from one.

docs.title: Writing to a manufacturer
docs.text:
The notebook answers the questions a support engineer asks first. Add what it cannot know:

  • the installation — engine, propeller and controller models and serials, firmware versions, the avionics that wrote the logs;
  • what you felt in the aircraft, when, and in what conditions;
  • the one question you want answered.

Keep the finding's count as EIS wrote it (in 93 of 98 takeoffs); it is the most persuasive thing in the message.

docs.title: What a finding is not
docs.text:
It is not an airworthiness judgement, and Research does not make one. Whether a repeating rpm shape is acceptable for flight is answered by the Operators Manual's limits (which the app checks separately, under Limits and events), by the manufacturers of the engine and the governing parts, and by you.

Spec 06 §10.3 and Spec 16 §5 define the ways out.

docs.title: Investigations: asking Claude about your engine
docs.text: In brief. You look at your flights in EIS and mark what looks odd; with the EIS extension installed in Claude Desktop, you ask Claude — Investigate, with no text, takes your newest marked question — and Claude investigates: it starts from your marks, measures across your flights with the EIS instrument, writes code against your logs where no measurement fits, reads the manuals you've given it, and writes what it found into EIS as a notebook you can read, re-run and share. Your logs stay on your computer. Claude investigates; EIS measures.

docs.title: What an investigation is
docs.text:
The oscillation case — 180 rpm of cycling on nearly every takeoff, inside every limit, unchanged for 145 hours — was found by a loop: cut every full-power segment, notice manifold pressure moving in step with rpm, read the engine manual's boost schedule, form a hypothesis about the governor and the boost control arguing, test it against altitude, rule out two other explanations, and write it up so the propeller manufacturer recognised it from one email. The measurements took minutes; the loop took judgement. Claude did the loop, with the owner steering.

An investigation is that loop, done by your Claude with EIS as its instrument. You bring what you saw and the question; Claude does the measuring, reading and writing; you steer and decide.

You look and mark, in EIS a flight with Signal on · zoom to what looks odd · Mark for Claude: the window, your note, a question Research → Inbox keeps your questions Claude Desktop your account, your conversation You ask “look into my marks” You steer “compare every takeoff” Claude decides what to do next and says what it is doing EIS on your computer — the instrument Look one flight first: a log view, its signal Measure across the flights: slices, tests, code Read your manuals, your aircraft notes Explain a hypothesis, alternatives ruled out again, until the question is answered The notebook, in your workspace each step a cell: what was done, its output, what it means your logs and workspace — read by the engine, never sent anywhere results Claude calls tools; it never opens a log file. The numbers in the notebook are the engine's. Look and mark in EIS, ask in Claude Desktop, read the notebook in EIS.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The Claude Desktop app on a Mac, with your own Claude account. EIS runs no AI itself and holds no key: the conversation is yours, on your account.
  • The EIS extension for Claude Desktop — one file, one install (Install the extension). It carries the EIS engine, runs the EIS pages on your computer at http://127.0.0.1:8420/ while Claude Desktop is open, and gives Claude its connection to them.
  • Your logs in a folder EIS can read, as on the website. If you started on the website, its Move my workspace to EIS on this computer button brings your questions, marks and decisions across (Install the extension, step 4); after the move you work at http://127.0.0.1:8420/, and the website's workspace is the copy.
  • Context worth giving it, in Settings → Aircraft (Set up your aircraft and documents): the aircraft's configuration and notes on what was changed and when, which Claude reads before every investigation; and documents folders with your copies of the Operators Manual, service bulletins and the propeller and controller manuals, which Claude reads in place and cites by page. EIS never ships the manuals and never copies them.

docs.title: How it goes
docs.text:
1. Look and mark. On a flight, turn on Signal under the chart, zoom to what looks odd, and Mark for Claude — a sentence of what you see, under a question. Mark the same thing on other flights under the same question (Mark something for Claude). You can skip this and just ask.
  2. Ask. In Claude Desktop, open a chat and choose Investigate from the chat's + menu. With no text it takes your newest open question; with text that names one of your questions it takes that one; anything else is a new question in your words — "the climb after my touch-and-go at KBLI on Oct 24 felt like a surge; look into it."
  3. Claude works. A notebook opens with your marks — your note, then a log view of each window — and Claude starts from what you saw. You see its steps in the chat and the notebook forming on the Research page. It measures what the question is about: whether something swings and repeats, whether two channels move together, whether a measurement differs before and after a change, which flights stand out — or, for anything else, it loads the data and plots it (What EIS measures).
  4. Steer. "Compare with every other takeoff." "Does it depend on altitude?" "What does the controller manual say about its governing band?"
  5. Read. The notebook in EIS, answer first: the question and its scope, what the data shows and what it means, and the proposed actions — who would do what, and what it would settle. Below that, the findings, each a sentence with its numbered table, figure or log view (the Flight view's chart for the window that matters, with Open flight), the calculation folded; then how it was done (Notebooks you keep and share). When Claude finishes, your question is marked watching (or what Claude and you decided), with the notebook linked from it.

A notebook is an ordinary Jupyter notebook. It opens unchanged in JupyterLab, where you can run it yourself against your workspace (Run a notebook in JupyterLab), and Re-run on the Research page runs it again on your current flights, holding any output that changed for you to accept or discard. Everything else — export as a zip or a page, keep or discard changed outputs, delete — is under Actions. On the website, notebooks open and read the same way; running them needs EIS on your computer.

docs.title: Research home
docs.text:
The Research page lists your notebooks as cards, newest first, with the inbox below them.

A card says what the notebook is without opening it: where it started (✎ your marks, ◉ something EIS raised, ? a question asked in Claude Desktop, ↓ imported), its title and status, the question, the channels it looked at in the Flight view's colours, how many flights over which dates, its evidence (∿ log views, ◫ figures, ▦ tables), the tests it ran (↻ cycling, ⇄ coupling, ⊟ groups, ◇ unusual), whether its outputs are current, and two or three topic words Claude gave it. Hover over any mark for its name; click a topic word to show only the notebooks that carry it. With more than six notebooks, a row above the cards filters them to Open or Finished. The statuses everywhere on the page are one dot and one word: new, investigating, watch, acted, nothing here for questions and what EIS raised; open, finished, reopened for notebooks, a finished notebook's dot coloured by what it concluded.

docs.title: The inbox
docs.text:
The inbox holds two kinds of thing, with the same statuses, one line each — open items first, what you've resolved behind Show resolved. Click a line to open it in place.

Your questions, with their marks across flights. An open question shows each mark with its time (Jan 1 · 12:01–12:03 (+1:50 into the flight); hover for the full time and zone), its channels and your note; each mark opens its flight at the window, with the channels you were looking at. The ⋯ menu on a question renames, resolves or deletes it; on a mark it edits the note, moves the mark to another question (or to Unassigned) or deletes it. A question Claude has taken up has Open the investigation.

What EIS raised. When the Research page opens after new flights, EIS runs its own cheap scan — no AI — over the preset slices of the recent flights and keeps only patterns that hold across many of them: a repeating cycle in governed rpm, a measurement that has moved against your reference, a group of slices that stands apart. Opened, each says what fired, with Show the evidence for the table (every slice, each opening its flight at that moment). The Look at this inbox item prompt in Claude Desktop takes one.

Mark either kind Nothing here, Watch or Acted, with a note, from its ⋯ menu. Nothing here is a legitimate result. How much the scan raises is Settings → Research → Inbox sensitivity: quiet (a pattern in 8 of the last 10 slices), normal (6 of 10, the default) or curious (4 of 10). On the website the inbox works the same, and an open question carries a line on handing it to Claude with the extension.

The scan never puts anything on a flight's cards, and a single odd flight is not a scan item — that is what your own marks are for. EIS never says what a pattern means; that is the investigation's.

docs.title: What stays true
docs.text:
• No verdicts. A notebook says what the data did, how big, how often, compared with what; it never says fault or abnormal without the reference beside it. The judgement is yours, with the Operators Manual and the people who built the parts.
  • Traceable. Every claim in a notebook comes from a measurement, a code cell's output, or a cited document — or it is labelled a hypothesis. The code is there to read.
  • Your marks are yours. A mark holds a flight, a window, the channels shown and your sentence. EIS adds nothing to it; Claude reads it as what you saw, not as a finding.
  • Private. Logs never leave your computer. What travels is what Claude asked the instrument for, inside your own conversation.
  • Fenced on a Mac — and only there. On a Mac, macOS itself fences in the code Claude runs on your computer: it can't reach the internet, start other programs, or change any file outside its own study folder. That fence exists only on a Mac, and the macOS tool it uses is one Apple has deprecated, though it still works today; on Windows and Linux only EIS's own, weaker check applies. On every computer the code can read any file you can, and what it reads can end up in your conversation with Claude.

docs.title: What to do with this
docs.text: Next time something feels odd in flight, find it on the flight with Signal on, mark it, and choose Investigate. Reproducing a takeoff investigation walks the original case that way.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: The extension bundles the EIS engine, a Python of its own, the EIS pages and an MCP server — the standard way Claude Desktop talks to local tools — in one process that Claude Desktop starts and stops. The pages see the same workspace, so a notebook cell written by Claude appears in your browser as it is written, and a mark you make appears to Claude at once. Claude calls tools: read your questions and marks, find flights, read channels, cut slices, run a test, run Python against the workspace, read a document from your folders, append a notebook cell (the tools, the prompts, the eis library, the notebook format). Claude never opens a log file; the engine answers tool calls. The design is Spec 16 — Investigations; the instrument it drives is Spec 06 — Research.

docs.title: Questions Research will ask next
docs.text:
In brief. EIS measures four kinds of question today. Six more are designed and will become instruments as they are built and measured against real logs. Until then Claude can ask any of them in a notebook with its own code against your logs — the instrument makes them faster, referenced and comparable, not possible.

Question What it would tell you Is this response damped, or self-sustaining? Whether a wobble dies away after a disturbance (a controller settling) or keeps going by itself (a limit cycle, as in the oscillation case) Is this what the Operators Manual says it should be? How far manifold pressure, fuel flow or temperatures sit from the Manual's engine deck for that rpm and altitude When did it change within the flight? The moment a signal's level or steadiness shifted inside a slice — a step in one EGT, an oil-pressure step Is this cylinder behaving like the others? One cylinder's EGT with the engine-wide movement removed, so its own dips and drift stand out Does it depend on conditions? How a measurement varies with density altitude, outside air temperature or wind Is the sensor or log healthy? Dropouts, stuck values, step sizes and noise, by log source

Each will follow the rules of the four that exist (What EIS measures): a count, a reference beside every number, no verdict. Research will not acquire thresholds of its own or grade findings by severity. If one of these is the one you need, the feedback board is the place to say so.

Spec 06 §7.5 specifies the six; §14 the scan and the shared detectors that may follow.

docs.title: Notebooks you keep and share
docs.text: In brief. Every investigation is a notebook, laid out so the answer comes first: the question, what the data shows and what it means, and the proposed actions; then the findings, each a sentence with the table, figure or log view it rests on; then how it was done. Your marks are there when it took up one of your questions. Notebooks are saved in the workspace and listed on the Research page with who wrote them and their finding. A notebook refers to flights by their fingerprint, never by file, so it travels: export it, and another owner imports it, reads your investigation, and with EIS on their computer runs it on their flights.

docs.title: What a notebook holds
docs.text:
A notebook has seven sections, always in this order. The first three are what to read when you have five minutes:

  1. The question — as asked, and its scope: which flights were looked at, which manual pages were used, what was taken as given, what the logs can't tell.
  2. Answer — What the data shows, three to five sentences, each with its count (in 93 of 98 takeoffs); and What it means — a hypothesis, how sure Claude is, and what would change its mind.
  3. Proposed actions — numbered, each saying what to do, who would do it (you, your mechanic, a manufacturer), what it would settle, and when EIS can watch it, re-check after the next N flights. Or None, and why.
  4. Findings — each one a sentence and the evidence it rests on: a table, a figure or a log view (the Flight view's chart for a window, with Open flight), numbered Table 1, Figure 2, Log view 3, with a caption saying what it shows. The calculation behind it is folded under show the calculation.
  5. How this was done — the plan, the data and how flights were cut into slices, the method, the alternatives ruled out, and anything from outside your logs labelled as context.
  6. Follow-ups — dated, when Claude came back to the notebook; each ends with what changed above.
  7. Working — the exploring Claude did on the way, kept but folded.

Sections 1–3 are written when Claude finishes, from what it states as the answer — not left as prose somewhere in the middle. The notebook also holds the files a cell wrote (a CSV, a figure) and a header: who wrote it, its status, how many actions it proposes, the engine version, and whether its outputs are current for this workspace. Notebooks written before 1.1.2 have no sections; they read as they always did.

It does not hold your logs. A log view draws its window from the flight in your workspace; where that flight is absent, it shows the picture saved with the notebook.

Full-power rpm cycle by claude · finished · 2 actions · outputs current for this workspace 1 The question — and its scope: flights, manuals, limits 2 Answer — what the data shows, 3–5 sentences with counts: • rpm cycles every 4.4 s in 10 of 10 takeoffs, swing 180 rpm What it means — a hypothesis, how sure, what would change it 3 Proposed actions — what · who · what it settles · or None 4 Findings The cycle is there on every takeoff, not one flight. Open flight Log view 1 — the full-power minute, on every takeoff ▸ show the calculation 5 How this was done plan, method, alternatives ruled out 6 Follow-ups dated; each ends with what changed above ▸ 7 Working (12 cells) The Answer, read first written when Claude finishes; earlier Answers folded inside Evidence a sentence, then its table, figure or log view — numbered, with a caption How it was reached so you can check it, or disagree The exploring, kept but folded One .ipynb file: the Research page, JupyterLab, an exported page A notebook on the Research page: the Answer first, then findings with their numbered evidence, how it was done, and the exploring folded at the end.

It is an ordinary Jupyter .ipynb: it opens in JupyterLab or VS Code, and runs there against your workspace (Run a notebook in JupyterLab).

docs.title: Keeping
docs.text: Notebooks live in the workspace and travel with a workspace export. On the Research page, Re-run (with EIS on your computer) runs every code cell again on your current flights; outputs that changed wait for you to Accept or Discard, cell by cell or all at once. That is the cheap way to ask the same question next season. Delete… removes a notebook and its files.

docs.title: Following up
docs.text: The conversation is where you and Claude think out loud; the notebook is what stays. Analysis Claude relies on goes into the notebook as a cell; exploring goes under Working; a quick look to decide where to go next stays in the chat. A cell that fails is fixed in place, not left behind a working copy, and Claude cannot finish while one is still failing. When you talk on after a notebook is finished and the answer changes — a new measurement, an alternative ruled out — Claude adds a dated follow-up under Follow-ups, ending with what changed, and finishes the notebook again. While it works the notebook reads reopened; afterwards the new Answer is on top and the earlier one is folded inside it, with its date. Say "put that in the notebook" whenever you want something kept. Facts about the aircraft — a part changed, a setting — belong in your notes in Settings → Aircraft; Claude asks you to add them there.

docs.title: Sharing
docs.text:
Two exports, on the notebook's page:

  • Export notebook (.zip) — the notebook and its files. Flights are named by fingerprint — a code derived from each log, meaningless to anyone who does not hold the same log.
  • Export as a page (.html) — one self-contained page anyone can open in a browser, with no EIS at all: the narrative, outputs, figures and log-view pictures. The one to send a mechanic or a manufacturer.

Someone who receives the .zip (or a bare .ipynb) chooses Import a notebook… on their Research page. EIS matches its flights against their workspace: cells whose flights are here are live; cells whose flights are absent show the sender's outputs, read-only, and say so.

docs.title: Run this on my flights
docs.text:
An imported notebook has one more button: Run this on my flights. It copies the notebook as a new one in your workspace — … — my flights — and, with EIS on your computer, runs every code cell against your own flights and keeps the outputs. Now the same measurements are about your engine, beside the sender's.

This is how a finding spreads without anyone's logs moving: here is the notebook that found the oscillation on my aircraft — run it on yours. The receiving owner's data never leaves their machine, and the sender's never had to.

docs.title: What to do with this
docs.text: Keep a notebook even when it says something dull; re-running it next season is free. Before sending one, export it as a page and read it as the recipient will. When you receive one, run it on your flights before reading the sender's conclusions too closely.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Notebooks live in the workspace's studies/<id>/ folder (notebook.ipynb and files/) and are carried by workspace export. Their EIS metadata — author, status, question, summary, the inbox item or question it answered — sits in the notebook's own metadata (The notebook format). Import always creates a new notebook. Notebooks made before Research became notebook-only open as notebooks, converted on first load.

Spec 16 — Investigations §5 defines the notebook, its export and import.

docs.title: Research: the third question
docs.text: In brief. The app asks three questions of your engine. Did a value cross an Operators Manual line? — that is Limits and events. Has a value been drifting over the months? — that is Trends. Research asks the third: within a flight, does each signal behave the way it should — and does it do so on every flight? It works one way: Claude investigates; EIS measures. You look at a flight in EIS with Signal on, mark what looks odd for Claude, ask in Claude Desktop, and read the notebook Claude writes back into EIS. EIS never tells you something is wrong; it measures, and keeps the evidence.

docs.title: Three questions, three blind spots
docs.text:
Each question sees what the other two cannot.

Limits: did it cross a line? OM limit inside the limit — nothing to report Trends: is it drifting? flight after flight, the same the same since the first flight — nothing to report Research: what shape does it have? period swing a repeating shape, on every flight Three questions, three blind spots: a limit sees level, a trend sees drift, Research sees shape.
  • A limit is a line. A signal that stays under it is invisible to the limit checker, however oddly it moves.
  • A trend compares your engine with its own past. A behaviour your engine has had since the first flight is, to Trends, normal.
  • Research looks at the shape of a signal within a flight — steady or swinging, leading or lagging, like the other flights or not — and asks the same of every flight you have.

The case that made this page necessary: one aircraft's rpm cycled up and down by about 180 rpm every four seconds on nearly every takeoff, for 145 engine hours. It stayed inside every limit, so no event fired. It never changed, so no trend moved. It was felt once, in calm air, and found by asking Claude to line up every full-power segment of every flight, read the engine's manual, and test what it found. That loop — look, measure, read, hypothesise, eliminate, write up — is what Research is for. Claude does the loop; EIS is the instrument it uses and the record it keeps.

docs.title: Look, mark, ask, read
docs.text:
You look and mark, in EIS a flight with Signal on · zoom to what looks odd · Mark for Claude: the window, your note, a question Research → Inbox keeps your questions Claude Desktop your account, your conversation You ask “look into my marks” You steer “compare every takeoff” Claude decides what to do next and says what it is doing EIS on your computer — the instrument Look one flight first: a log view, its signal Measure across the flights: slices, tests, code Read your manuals, your aircraft notes Explain a hypothesis, alternatives ruled out again, until the question is answered The notebook, in your workspace each step a cell: what was done, its output, what it means your logs and workspace — read by the engine, never sent anywhere results Claude calls tools; it never opens a log file. The numbers in the notebook are the engine's. You look and mark in EIS; you ask in Claude Desktop; Claude works through EIS and writes the notebook.
  1. Look. Open a flight and turn on Signal under its chart. Under each channel a strip shows how far it swings, second by second, and where it repeats. Zoom to a stretch and its numbers appear beside their Operators Manual references: the swing, the period, how the other channels move with it.
  2. Mark. Something looks odd? With the chart zoomed to it, Mark for Claude: a sentence of what you see, and the question it belongs to — a new one with a title, one you already have, or none for now. A mark keeps where to look and your note; nothing is measured. Your questions and their marks gather in the inbox on the Research page (Mark something for Claude).
  3. Ask. In Claude Desktop, choose the Investigate prompt. With no text it takes your newest open question and starts from your marks; or ask in your own words. Claude finds the flights, measures across them, reads your manuals and notes, and steers by what you say (Investigations).
  4. Read. The notebook appears on the Research page as Claude writes it. When it is finished it opens on the answer: the question and its scope, what the data shows with its counts, what it means, and what to do about it — then the findings with their evidence, and how it was done. Keep it, re-run it next season, export it, share it (Notebooks you keep and share).

Asking needs the EIS extension in Claude Desktop, on your computer. On the website you can look, mark and read; your questions wait in the inbox, and the page says how to hand them to Claude.

docs.title: What EIS measures
docs.text: Claude chooses what to measure; the numbers are EIS's. The instrument cuts flights into slices — every takeoff, every climb, the window you marked — measures each one (level, spread, swing, period, how channels move together), and answers four kinds of question with a count and a reference beside every number: is it steady?, do these move together?, are these groups different?, which flights stand out? Claude uses those when the question is one of them, and writes its own code against your logs when it is not. What EIS measures is the fine print.

docs.title: The inbox
docs.text: You don't have to notice something to start. When the Research page opens after new flights, EIS runs its own scan — no AI — over the recent flights and keeps only patterns that hold across many of them. Those wait in the inbox beside your own questions, with the same statuses: new, investigating, nothing here, watching, acted on.

docs.title: What Research does not do
docs.text:
It brings no rules of its own. The only numbers the app contributes are Operators Manual values already in your engine profile; everything else is measured from your own flights or named with its source. It declares nothing abnormal, faulty or detected. It changes nothing elsewhere in the app until you take a finding somewhere — into the Journal, or to the person who can act on it (From a finding to action).

A repeating shape in a signal may be a problem, a characteristic of the installation, or nothing. Research gives you the evidence to ask the right person; it does not pretend to be that person.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Everything Research does is an operation of the EIS engine, the same on the website and on your computer; Claude reaches the same operations as tools through the extension, so a number in a notebook is the number the page would show. Cutting slices reads the logs again — the normal analysis keeps only per-flight results — so a first measurement over a whole workspace takes some seconds.

The instrument is Spec 06 — Research; investigations, marks and the inbox are Spec 16 — Investigations. The case that shaped both is the owner's takeoff RPM/MAP oscillation investigation.

docs.title: Sharing a workspace
docs.text: In brief. Settings → App → Export workspace… writes a file you can send to another pilot, your mechanic, or someone helping you read your engine. It carries your settings and decisions and — with Include logs — the logs themselves, so the recipient opens it and sees exactly what you see. Anonymise logs replaces the aircraft identity with a pseudonym and blanks the position and radio data. The recipient uses Import workspace… and gets a new workspace of their own.

docs.title: Why export a whole workspace
docs.text: The export is also how a workspace moves between browsers or computers, and your backup against the browser clearing its storage — the same file does all three. The useful thing to share is rarely one number. It is "look at this engine" — the flights, the way the limits have been tolerated, the trend that worried you. A workspace export carries all of that in one file, so the person at the other end sees your Flight views, your Trends and your Journal rather than a screenshot and a description.

docs.title: What the export contains
docs.text:
Always: the workspace's settings, its reference and model settings, which flights are excluded and why, pinned references, every filter and rule edit, the Journal, your annotations, and a list of the flights in it. Not carried: the analysis results themselves (the recipient's app recomputes them from the logs), your folder paths, or anything about your computer.

With Include logs (on by default): the log files, zipped together with the workspace. Without them the export is a small file that describes a workspace but cannot show one; the recipient sees Link your logs to see this workspace's analysis. Sharing with the logs is the normal case.

With Anonymise logs: the tail number and avionics system ID are replaced by a pseudonym (one per aircraft), GPS position and the nav/com columns are blanked, and the files are renamed flight_001.csv, flight_002.csv … Dates, times and engine hours are not changed — they are what makes the analysis work. Nor is anything you typed: your notes, filter reasons and the workspace name go as written, and the export dialog lists where your tail number appears in them so you can edit first.

To share only some flights, make a workspace that points at a folder with just those logs, and export that.

Settings → App: export with or without logs, anonymised or not, with the privacy note.

docs.title: What the recipient gets
docs.text:
Import workspace… (under Settings → App, or from the workspace switcher) always creates a new workspace, named after yours with (imported) added. It first shows a summary — whose it is, which engine, how many flights, how many filters and rule edits — then unpacks the logs into a folder of its own and matches them against your flight list: 38 of 40 flights found · 2 missing · 12 other logs held out. Then the usual analysis runs.

The recipient sees your workspace as you saw it: your filters, your exclusions, your pins, your Journal. A flight whose log did not arrive is listed under Skipped as In the sender's workspace — log not found, and your decisions about it wait until the log appears. A log that was in the zip but not in your workspace — perhaps you had skipped it — is held out, listed with Include if they want it.

An import from a newer version of the app than the recipient is running is refused with a message; from an older one it proceeds with a notice.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
An engine log carries more than engine data: your tail number, your avionics' serial number, the date and time of every flight, and your GPS track. Anonymising removes the identity and the track; it leaves the dates and times, because trends over engine hours need them. If that is more than you want to share, share fewer flights. The app shows this notice every time you export.

Walkthrough: Export and import.

docs.title: The Journal
docs.text: In brief. The Journal lists every decision currently in force in the workspace — each filter, rule edit, excluded flight, pinned reference, changed setting, research finding and annotation — with what it is doing right now. It is a register, not a log: reverse a decision and its entry disappears; edit one and its entry updates. Anything that needs your attention — a filter that has been breached or is drifting, a decision that no longer does anything — floats to the top, and the count on the Journal item in the top bar tells you how many.

docs.title: Why a register and not a history
docs.text:
A pilot managing an aircraft wants to know what is in effect. Which limits have I tolerated, and within what bounds? Which rules have I changed from the defaults? Which flights are out of the reference, and why? A history of every change ever made answers a different question, and buries the first one. So the Journal keeps one entry per live decision and nothing else. There is no settings changelog; if a setting differs from the app's default, the Journal lists it with both values.

One line per decision, grouped by kind, each with what it is doing now. A research finding is expanded.

docs.title: How the page reads
docs.text:
Anything that needs you comes first, in a Needs a look block — and only when there is something in it. Below it, every decision is one line: a small mark for its kind, its title, what it is doing now in a few words (4 events · 4 flights, changes no verdict, +1 insight · 1 flight), and the date it was last changed. A decision that currently does nothing says so in grey with a hollow dot.

The lines are grouped by kind, each group under a header with its count and its total effect — 1 filter · hiding 4 events on 4 flights. Filters, exclusions, changed settings and research findings are open; annotations and acknowledgements start folded; a kind with nothing in it is not shown at all. Above the list, a search box finds a word in any title, reason, note or flight, and Group switches between by kind, by date and by flight.

Click a line and it opens in place: the value (your band, the new setting beside the shipped one), what it applies to, your reason and note in quotes, and when it was made and changed. The ⋯ menu at the end of the line holds the actions: Edit, the decision's reversal — Remove filter, Include again, Enable, Unpin, Reset to shipped, Remove from Journal — which first says what it would change, and Open the notebook for a research finding.

Manage limit filters → in the filters header opens each filter's full card — its status, how far past the limit and how long each flight went, and the reference it watches against — with Edit, Reset reference, Mark reviewed and Copy filters from… another workspace with the same engine.

A filter's card: status, its band, your note, and every flight's excess against the band.

docs.title: What is listed
docs.text:
Kind The line shows Opened, it adds Limit filter The limit, and the events and flights it hides now. Your band and duration, the phases it leaves out, your note; Remove filter. Excluded flight The flight, and whether excluding it changes a verdict. Your reason; Include again. Changed setting The setting, and the insights it changes. The value beside the shipped default; Reset to shipped. Rule edit The topic, and the insights the edit adds or removes. The trigger's value beside the shipped one; Reset to shipped. Disabled topic The topic, and the insights it would have raised. Enable. Pinned reference The metric, and how many flights it is pinned to. The pinned flights and your label; Unpin. Research finding The notebook's title and its finding in one sentence. The notebook's Answer; Open the notebook, Remove from Journal. Annotation The first line of your note. The whole note and what it is attached to; Delete. Acknowledged insight Reserved for single-insight acknowledgements, which are planned.

The counts are recomputed every time you open the page.

Research findings. When Claude finishes a notebook and you ask it to keep the finding, the Journal records the notebook's title and one sentence of what was found (From a finding to action). The line follows the notebook: if the notebook is reopened and finished again, the line is rewritten from it.

docs.title: Change notices
docs.text:
Some entries need you. They move to the top and are counted on the nav badge:

  • A filter that is breached or drifting (see Your decisions). The Flights page carries a one-line banner pointing here.
  • A decision with zero effect — a filter with nothing left to suppress, an exclusion that changes no verdict. Usually the cue to remove it.
  • A pinned reference older than the recent window — a reminder that the comparison is now against a fixed past.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text: Changing the display units, the data location or updating the app creates no entry; none of those affects any result. And the Journal never contains anything the app decided on its own, because the app does not make decisions — it only records yours.

docs.title: The topics
docs.text:
In brief. Eight topics have a card on every Flight view. Each one below says what it measures, what it is compared against, when its insight fires and what the insight can point to. The text is the same as behind the ? on each card, with the Operators Manual values filled in for the 916iS; on a 915iS or 912iS the card shows that engine's values. The status line says on which engines the topic has been validated with real data.

Every topic was developed and validated on a Rotax 916iS. On the 915iS and 912iS the same analysis runs, but until logs from such an aircraft have confirmed it behaves sensibly there, the card carries Not yet validated on this engine. One topic does not exist on the 912iS at all, because the engine has no turbocharger.

Topic 916iS 915iS 912iS Cylinder balance (EGT spread) validated unverified unverified Cylinder EGT deviation validated unverified unverified Oil temperature peak validated unverified unverified Coolant temperature peak validated unverified unverified Time at takeoff power validated unverified unverified Turbo boost at takeoff validated unverified — Engine computer alerts in flight provisional unverified unverified Operators Manual limits validated unverified unverified

Provisional on the engine computer alerts means the sorting of alerts by phase has been checked against many flights, but no genuine in-flight alert has yet occurred in the data, so that case has not been seen for real.

docs.title: Cylinder balance (EGT spread)
docs.text:
Your engine computer sets the fuel and spark for each cylinder, so the four exhaust gas temperatures (EGTs) should keep a consistent pattern from flight to flight. This topic measures the spread between the hottest and the coolest cylinder in cruise. It compares that spread with your own past flights in similar outside air temperature, and with the Operators Manual limit of 392 °F (which applies when fuel flow is above 3 L/h, i.e. at any normal power setting). It also watches whether the spread is slowly growing as engine hours build up.

A widening spread can point to an injector, spark plug or ignition problem. A single unusual flight is worth noting; a spread that keeps growing over several flights is worth raising with your mechanic. When one cylinder on its own explains the change, it is reported under Cylinder EGT deviation instead, so you see it once.

Measured in: cruise. Compared with: your reference (same temperature band) and the OM split limit. Insight fires on: a flight outside your usual range, or a widening trend over engine hours. See Cylinder balance.

docs.title: Cylinder EGT deviation
docs.text:
Every engine has its own cylinder pattern, and on many one cylinder always runs hotter than the rest. Instead of judging cylinders against a generic ideal, this topic compares each cylinder's cruise EGT, measured against the average of the other three, with that same cylinder's own history. It flags a flight that is clearly outside the cylinder's usual range once there are at least 10 comparable flights, and a steady drift up or down as engine hours build up.

A cylinder running hotter than usual can mean a lean injector; one running cooler can point to ignition or a spark plug; erratic readings often point to the EGT probe itself. If the change also means a different cylinder is now the hottest, the message says so.

Measured in: cruise. Compared with: each cylinder's own reference (same temperature band). Insight fires on: a cylinder outside its usual range, or a trend in either direction.

docs.title: Oil temperature peak
docs.text:
This shows the highest oil temperature reached during the flight and compares it with your usual peak on flights in similar outside air temperature. Short flights often end before the engine is fully warm, so a lower peak after a short hop is normal.

A peak well above your usual can point to reduced oil cooling — less airflow through the oil cooler, a partial blockage, or a long climb on a hot day. A peak well below your usual on a full-length flight can mean the oil is not getting warm enough. If the oil went past the Operators Manual limit of 248 °F, that is reported once, under Operators Manual limits, and this card shows the same badge.

Measured over: the whole flight. Compared with: your reference (same temperature band). Insight fires on: a peak outside your usual range.

docs.title: Coolant temperature peak
docs.text:
