docs.title: Reporting a problem or suggesting a feature
docs.text: The feedback board is where bugs are reported and features are suggested and voted on. It needs no GitHub account, and the app opens it from the speech-bubble icon in its top bar or from Settings → App → About, beside the build line worth quoting in a report. For a problem with the analysis of a flight, the most useful thing you can offer is a workspace export — anonymised if you prefer.

docs.title: Asking an assistant
docs.text: Everything on this site is plain text in the repository under docs/. If you use an AI assistant, you can point it at the repository or paste the pages you are interested in and ask questions in your own words. The concept pages are written so that their opening In brief reads correctly out of context.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Aircraft log — The log a Garmin AXIS hands to Garmin Pilot, downloaded from flyGarmin as aircraft-log-<tail number>-<date and time>.csv. Always covers the whole power-up. When the same flight's AXIS card log is also present, the app keeps both and analyses this one.

Analysis line — The first line of every topic card: this flight's number, your usual, and the Operators Manual limit. Always present; never a judgement.

Blip — An engine-computer alert shorter than three seconds. Counted, never an event.

Breach — An event that a filter on that limit does not cover. Shown as an ordinary event, marked beyond your filter.

CAS event — An occurrence of a panel alert (today, the ENGINE ECU caution) that the app did not expect — on the ground with the engine running but not a lane check, or in flight. Listed with limit events.

Close call — Time at takeoff power within 60 seconds of the five-minute limit.

Contributing flight — A flight that is part of the reference. Every admitted flight contributes unless you exclude it.

Density altitude (DA) band — One of four altitude-and-temperature conditions (low, moderate, high, very high) within which cruise fuel figures and takeoff boost are compared.

Descriptor — One measurement of one channel over one slice: level, spread, swing, period, correlation with rpm, largest rate of change, and so on. The per-slice table is descriptors.

Deviation (cylinder) — One cylinder's cruise EGT minus the average of the other three.

Drifting — A filter whose recent flights have gone further past the limit, or had events more often, than the flights the filter was set against.

ECU — The engine control unit, the engine computer. Two lanes, A and B.

Effect size — How completely two groups of slices separate on a measurement, from 0 (interleaved) to 1 (no overlap). The headline of Are these two groups different?; shown instead of a probability.

Engine hours — The engine meter reading, carried in every log. The x-axis of every trend.

Event — A reading past an Operators Manual limit for long enough to matter, or an unexpected CAS alert: when, which phase, how long, how far.

Evidence — In a notebook, the table, figure or log view a finding rests on: numbered (Table 1), with a caption saying what it shows, the calculation folded beside it.

Evidence package — One file from a study: each question's finding, magnitude and reference, caveats, and the per-slice table. Written for someone who has never seen the app.

Exclude (from reference) — Keep a flight's own analysis but stop it shaping what other flights are compared with. Needs a reason.

FADEC — Full-authority digital engine control. On a Rotax iS the engine computer sets fuel and spark; the pilot has only the throttle.

Filter — Your statement that a limit is exceeded on your aircraft in a way you understand and accept, within bounds you set. Applies to every flight; still watched.

Finding — The one-sentence first part of a Research result, always with a count: in 93 of 98 slices. In a notebook, each finding is a sentence with its evidence; the first sentence of What the data shows is the one the Journal keeps.

Fingerprint (flight) — A code derived from a log's contents by which studies name flights. The same log gives the same fingerprint anywhere; nothing about the log can be recovered from it.

Flight facts — Fuel burned, cruise miles per gallon, cruise fuel flow and the lane-check result, shown in the Flight view header for planning. Never compared, never alerted.

Flight — A log the app has admitted: airborne for at least ten minutes, without a long gap, not a duplicate.

Hand slice — A slice of one flight and a window, named directly rather than cut by a rule — usually one of your marks.

Inbox — The panel on Research home holding your questions with their marks, and the patterns EIS's own scan raised across recent flights, each with a status.

Insight — A short statement on a topic card that something about this flight is worth your attention. Appears only when a trigger fires.

Journal — The register of every decision currently in force in the workspace.

Lag — The number of seconds one channel trails another at their best match. Zero means they move together.

Lane check — The pre-takeoff single-lane engine test. The app recognises it by RPM and pattern and reports whether both lanes were covered.

Limit — An Operators Manual operating limit for your engine model.

Log — A file your Garmin avionics wrote during one power-up: a G3X log, its Garmin Pilot export, an AXIS card log or an aircraft log.

Mark — A window of one flight, the channels shown and a sentence of what you saw, saved for Claude with Mark for Claude under one of your questions (or Unassigned). It holds no measurement.

Merge gap — In a slice rule, the longest dip in the conditions that does not split a slice in two.

n_min — How many other flights the reference needs before a comparison is made. Default 10.

Notebook — An investigation as a Jupyter .ipynb, in seven sections: the question, the Answer, proposed actions, findings with their evidence, how it was done, follow-ups, and the working, folded. Listed on the Research page; re-runs on your flights with EIS on your computer.

OAT band — One of four outside-air-temperature conditions (cold, mild, warm, hot) within which thermal metrics are compared.

Outlier — A flight more than the z-threshold (default 2 standard deviations) from your usual for a metric.

Period — Seconds per cycle of a repeating up-and-down in a channel. Below about 3 s nothing can be seen in once-a-second logs.

Phase — What the aircraft was doing at each second of a flight — pre-start, start, warm-up, taxi, takeoff roll, climb, cruise, descent, approach, landing roll, shutdown — worked out automatically.

Pin — Fix a metric's reference to a chosen set of flights instead of the rolling history.

Preset — A slice rule the app ships, measured against real logs: full-power segment, governed climb, stable cruise, idle, warm-up. Copy and edit freely.

Proposed action — In a notebook's Answer: what to do, who would do it, what it would settle, and when to re-check — or None, and why.

Question (yours) — A title that gathers your marks, listed in the inbox with a status (new, investigating, nothing here, watching, acted on). Investigate with no text takes the newest open one.

Read-only study — An imported study none of whose flights are in the workspace. Shows the sender's results under a clear label; Run this on my flights makes a study of yours from it.

Recent window — The newest flights Trends compares against the reference: at least the last 10 engine hours, at least 5 flights, at most 15.

Recurrence — In how many of a set's slices a finding holds, out of all of them. The first number to read.

Reference (Research) — What a magnitude is shown beside: an Operators Manual value from the engine profile, the spread across the set's own slices, or a value you typed in with a label and a source.

Reference — What the app has learned from your own flights about what each metric usually is on this engine: average and spread, by condition where it matters. Also your usual.

Research — The app's third question: within a flight, does each signal behave as it should, and on every flight? You look and mark in EIS, ask Claude, and read the notebook; Claude investigates, EIS measures.

Rolling — A reference that includes every earlier contributing flight and grows as you fly. The default.

Rule — A topic's triggers and their values. Editable from the card; one set per workspace.

Severity — The label on an event or insight: LIMIT, WARNING, WATCH, INFO (CAUTION on limits). A reading aid; the app does not act on it.

Shift — On Trends, the recent window's average sitting far enough from the reference's average to count as a change.

Skipped — A log that did not become a flight, listed with its reason. Can be included.

Reference row — In Compare, the row you pin. Every other row then shows its difference from it (Δ period, Δ swing, Δ correlation), and the chart marks it. Saved with the study.

Slice rule — Conditions on channels, a minimum duration, a merge gap and an optional phase, which together cut slices from every flight.

Slice set — All the slices a rule produces over a selection of flights. What every question is asked of.

Slice — A stretch of one flight cut by a rule, a phase or by hand, carrying every channel and its context. The unit of Research.

Spread (EGT) — Hottest cruise EGT minus coolest.

Standing out — Of a slice: sitting far from the other slices of the same source on some measurement. Different, not wrong.

Still building — The reference does not yet have n_min flights for this metric; the number is shown, the comparison withheld.

Storage — Where the app keeps your workspaces when it runs in your browser: the browser's private storage for the site, on this device. Shown under Settings → App. Logs are never kept there.

Strip — With Signal on in the Flight view, a band under a channel shaded along the flight: the swing strip shows how far the channel moves within a short sliding window, and the repeat strip lights where a period stands out.

Study — A notebook: an investigation saved in the workspace, with its question, narrative, code and outputs. Travels as a .zip or an .ipynb; see Notebook.

Swing — Bottom-to-top of a channel within a short window, as a median over the slice; the size of a cycle.

Sync — Rescan the workspace's folders for new or moved logs and offer to analyse them.

Topic — One thing the app watches, with a card on every Flight view.

Trend — A metric moving steadily with engine hours, reported only when a straight line fits well (R² ≥ 0.5) over at least ten flights.

Trigger — A condition on a topic that, when met, produces an insight: baseline deviation, trend or threshold.

Unverified / not yet validated — The topic runs on this engine model but no data from such an aircraft has yet confirmed it behaves sensibly.

Window (Signal) — The seconds of one flight the chart is zoomed to; with Signal on, its numbers appear beside their references, and Mark for Claude marks it.

Workspace — The app's view of one aircraft: its log folders plus everything derived and every decision made. Lives in the browser it was made in (or, when the app runs as a program, in its data folder); moves by export and import.

z-threshold — How many standard deviations from your usual a reading must be to count as unusual. Default 2.0.

docs.title: Investigation prompts
docs.text: The prompts the EIS extension offers in Claude Desktop (Spec 16 §4.6): pick one from the + menu in a chat, fill in what it asks, and Claude starts with the EIS method in front of it. Each is shown below as Claude receives it, with the placeholders in braces.

docs.title: Investigate
docs.text:
Investigate a question about the engine in a notebook, following the EIS method.

Asks for question The question, in your words (e.g. "Is there an oscillation during takeoff and initial climb?"), or the title of one you marked on the Flight view; leave it empty and Claude takes your newest open question The prompt

Investigate this question about my engine with SlingologyEIS:

{{question}}

Which question: call guide first — it lists the questions I marked on the Flight view (Mark for Claude). If the question above is empty, take my newest open question (pins_list names it newest_open); if I have none, ask me what to investigate — you may suggest what my open inbox candidates (inbox_list) and recent flights point to — and wait for my answer. If the text above names one of my questions (its title, or near it), take that one. Otherwise it is a new question in my words.

  1. Call guide first and follow its method and writing rules.
  2. Find the flight or flights the question names with flights_find (or flights_list), and read aircraft_get — my notes say what changed and when.
  3. Start a notebook with study_create: for one of my questions pass its question_id, and the notebook opens with my marks — my note, then a log view of the window — so start from what I saw; otherwise the question as I asked it. Write the plan under How this was done ("section": 5) before you measure.
  4. Look at one flight first (a log view of the window, eis.load), then across all my flights with a slice rule, measuring what the question is about — the guide's table says which instrument fits (a test only when the question is about steadiness, coupling, a difference or an outlier; otherwise load, slice, plot and look). Each finding is one sentence and one evidence cell (eis.table, eis.figure, a log view, each with a caption); a test used for another reason says why beside it. Explore in scratch cells.
  5. Read what my manuals say about it (documents_list, document_read) and cite the pages. Anything from outside my logs and documents (forums, other owners) is context, under How this was done, labelled so.
  6. State the mechanism as a hypothesis and name the alternatives you ruled out, each with its evidence, under How this was done.
  7. Finish with the structured Answer: study_finish with question_scope (flights and dates, references, what was taken as given, what the logs can't tell), shows (3–5 sentences with numbers — the first is my Journal's line), means (the hypothesis, your confidence, what would change it) and actions (what · who · what it would settle; recheck_after_flights when EIS can watch it; or actions_none and why); question when it was one of mine, so it and its marks are resolved; tags: two or three topic words for what the notebook is about (not what it found).

The notebook is the record (the guide's The notebook is the record): every finding is one sentence and one evidence cell (eis.table, eis.figure or a log view, with a caption — never a print); the plan and the method go under How this was done; exploring is scratch. A quick look to decide where to go next is a probe and stays in the chat. If we talk on after you finish and it changes what the notebook says — or I say "put that in the notebook" — open a follow-up (study_followup), add its cells, and study_finish again with the Answer rewritten as it now stands and changed saying what changed above.

Finish with the structured Answer.

docs.title: Look at this inbox item
docs.text:
Investigate one candidate the EIS detectors raised and resolve it.

Asks for candidate_id required — The inbox candidate's id (inbox_list shows them) The prompt

Look at inbox candidate {{candidate_id}} for me.

  1. Call guide first and follow its method.
  2. Read the candidate with inbox_list: its preset, measurement, the slices involved and the evidence.
  3. Start a notebook with study_create, passing inbox_candidate: "{{candidate_id}}", and write the plan under How this was done.
  4. Look at one of its slices in one flight (a log view), then measure across the flights what the candidate raised (the same preset, the same measurement — the guide's table names its instrument) and check the alternatives that fit it: one log source only, one flight only, the 1 Hz sampling floor for a period, altitude or temperature.
  5. Finish with the structured Answer — study_finish with question_scope, shows, means, actions (or actions_none) — resolving the candidate (resolution: nothing-here, watch or acted) with a one-line note saying why.

The notebook is the record (the guide's The notebook is the record): every finding is one sentence and one evidence cell (eis.table, eis.figure or a log view, with a caption — never a print); the plan and the method go under How this was done; exploring is scratch. A quick look to decide where to go next is a probe and stays in the chat. If we talk on after you finish and it changes what the notebook says — or I say "put that in the notebook" — open a follow-up (study_followup), add its cells, and study_finish again with the Answer rewritten as it now stands and changed saying what changed above.

docs.title: Before / after
docs.text:
Compare the engine before and after a change (a date, or the change in words).

Asks for change required — The date of the change (YYYY-MM-DD) or the change in words (e.g. "the new propeller") The prompt

Compare my engine before and after this change: {{change}}.

  1. Call guide first and follow its method.
  2. If I gave the change in words, find its date in my notes (aircraft_get) or the Journal (journal_list); if you can't, ask me.
  3. Start a notebook with study_create, and write the plan under How this was done before measuring.
  4. For the conditions the change could affect (full power, governed climb, stable cruise), compare the slices before and after with groups split by date — eis.groups("full_power", "rpm.swing", by="date", date="…") — for the measurements the change could have moved (for a propeller: rpm, its swing and period, MAP, fuel flow; for an oil change: oil temperature and pressure). Say why each measurement was chosen.
  5. Each thing that changed or did not is a finding: one sentence with its numbers and the group sizes, and its evidence table. The caveats (fewer flights after, different seasons or sources) go in question_scope. Finish with the structured Answer — study_finish with question_scope, shows, means and actions (or actions_none).

The notebook is the record (the guide's The notebook is the record): every finding is one sentence and one evidence cell (eis.table, eis.figure or a log view, with a caption — never a print); the plan and the method go under How this was done; exploring is scratch. A quick look to decide where to go next is a probe and stays in the chat. If we talk on after you finish and it changes what the notebook says — or I say "put that in the notebook" — open a follow-up (study_followup), add its cells, and study_finish again with the Answer rewritten as it now stands and changed saying what changed above.

docs.title: Review new flights
docs.text:
A short review of the flights since the last study finding, the inbox, and anything that stands out.

The prompt

Review my new flights.

  1. Call guide first.
  2. Find the flights since my last study finding (journal_list shows the study findings; flights_list with date_from), and read the inbox (inbox_list) and the questions I marked (pins_list).
  3. Start a short notebook with study_create ("Review of flights since …").
  4. For each new flight: one line on where it went and anything that stands out (events, Trends shifts, and eis.unusual — this review is about what stands out). For each open inbox candidate and each open question of mine: what it is, and whether it needs a closer look (Investigate takes a question).
  5. Finish with the structured Answer, briefly: shows — what stands out; means — what needs a closer look and what doesn't; actions — each closer look as what · who · what it would settle, or actions_none.

The notebook is the record (the guide's The notebook is the record): every finding is one sentence and one evidence cell (eis.table, eis.figure or a log view, with a caption — never a print); the plan and the method go under How this was done; exploring is scratch. A quick look to decide where to go next is a probe and stays in the chat. If we talk on after you finish and it changes what the notebook says — or I say "put that in the notebook" — open a follow-up (study_followup), add its cells, and study_finish again with the Answer rewritten as it now stands and changed saying what changed above.

docs.title: Investigation tools
docs.text:
The tools the EIS extension gives Claude (Spec 16 §4.2). Claude calls them; you don't need to — this page is for reading what Claude can and cannot do, and for checking a tool from the command line with slingology-eis mcp call TOOL '{…}', which prints the same JSON Claude receives.

Every result is {engine_version, workspace_id, result}. Tools marked writes change something in the workspace (a notebook, the inbox, the workspace used for the conversation); the others only read. None reaches the internet. A refusal is an error whose text says why and what to ask instead.

35 tools, in the order Claude sees them.

Tool What it does guide How to investigate with EIS, in one document: the method (one flight first, then across the flights; the mechanism as a hypothesis; alternatives ruled out; what it means and what to do; no verdict words without their reference), the tool map with every parameter form and an example, the notebook rules, this aircraft's record and the owner's notes, its documents, and the workspace in use (flights, date span, open inbox candidates) workspaces_list The aircraft's workspaces (and any other aircraft's), with the one these tools use workspace_use writes Use another of the aircraft's workspaces for the rest of this conversation (not the EIS pages) flights_list The workspace's flights, oldest first: local date and start/end time with the zone, route (airports resolved from GPS), takeoffs and landings, the pilot's name, engine hours, source (G3X or AXIS), flight facts, minutes per phase and event count flights_find Flights for a description in words, best first (at most 10), each with what matched: dates ("Oct 24", "2026-10-24", "last Friday", a month or weekday), airports by code or name ("KBLI", "Bellingham"), counts ("three landings", "two stops", "touch and go"), words of the pilot's flight name flight_get One flight: header, phases, flight facts, events (limit exceedances and CAS) and the topic findings the Flight view shows series_get Channels of one flight over a window (seconds from the log's start) fleet_metrics The Spec 12 per-flight metrics table (one row per flight, ordered by engine hours) with each metric's baseline, trend, outliers and shift; 50 rows per page trends_summary The Trends change summary (ranked metrics with baseline, trend and shift) and the shift history. presets_list The engine profile's shipped slice rules (Spec 06): id, name, the question each is for, its conditions. slices_build The slices a selection and slice rules make, each with its local time, context and descriptors; 50 per page samples_get The 1 Hz samples of slices, aligned at an anchor (crossing, start, end, peak:CHANNEL) question_run A Spec 06 test over a slice set — cycling, coupling, groups or unusual — with its finding, magnitude with OM references, caveats and the evidence rows (50 per page) signal_analyze One flight's rolling strips, summarised as the runs where each channel cycles (lit), and a window's descriptors, numbers with OM references and diagnostics (periods, the 5 strongest periodogram peaks, best lag) and caveats rows_compare One row per slice, grouped by flight, with deltas to a pinned row; 50 rows per page code_run writes Run Python on the bench and keep it as a code cell in the notebook study_id (study_create first: every executed cell belongs to a notebook) — appended, or replacing cell_id profile_get The engine profile: limits with their Operators Manual references. aircraft_get The aircraft record: name, airframe, engine serial, propeller, controller, firmware, avionics, the documents folders; the owner's notes (notes.md) whole; its workspaces; the engine model and the Settings → Log channels assignments. documents_list The aircraft's documents — the Operators Manual, service bulletins, manuals, notes — read in place from the folders the owner named (Settings → Aircraft → Documents folders; subfolders included): name, folder, kind, pages, first line document_read Pages of one document (at most 3 at a time), or the pages where a phrase occurs (find: case-insensitive, accents ignored, with snippets) journal_list The Journal entries as the UI shows them; 50 per page. studies_list The notebooks in the workspace, newest first: kind, author, question, status, finding, and each one's card — origin, channels, flights and dates, evidence, tests, outputs, resolution, tags. study_read One study: a notebook's metadata (question, status, summary) and its cells with their outputs (figures named, not drawn; pending re-run outputs flagged). study_create writes Start an investigation notebook for a question; its first cell holds the question cell_append writes Append a cell to a notebook, at the end of its section: markdown (source) — a finding's one sentence, what a result means, the plan; code (source, run at once, as code_run); logview (flight, start_s, end_s, channels, marks [[t_s, "label"], …], title, caption) — a strip chart of a window of one flight that the EIS pages open as the Flight view (evidence by default) study_rerun writes Re-run every code cell of a notebook against this workspace; outputs that differ wait as pending until study_accept or study_discard. study_accept writes Accept the pending re-run outputs (all, or cell_ids): they become the cells' outputs study_discard writes Discard the pending re-run outputs (all, or cell_ids); the stored outputs stand study_finish writes End an investigation with its Answer, which EIS writes as sections 1–3: question_scope (the flights and dates looked at, the references used, what was taken as given, what the logs can't tell — a short list), shows (3–5 sentences, each a number the data shows; shows[0] is the Journal's line), means (the hypothesis, confidence in words, what would change the view), actions ([{what, who, settles, recheck_after_flights?}], or [] with actions_none saying why) study_followup writes Open a dated follow-up in a notebook (section 6): later cells appended without a section land in it, and study_finish closes it with changed — what changed above cell_edit writes Change a cell's role (code: evidence, support, scratch; markdown: narrative, scratch), move it to the end of a section (4 Findings, 5 How this was done, 6 Follow-ups, 7 Working), or replace a markdown cell's text inbox_list The candidates the detectors raised (recurring patterns, stand-out flights, shifts, groups) with evidence and status; scans first when there are new flights inbox_resolve writes Set a candidate's status — investigating, nothing-here, watch, acted (or new) — with its study and a note pins_list The owner's questions and marks (Mark for Claude on the Flight view): each question with its status, notebook and marks — flight, window (start_s, end_s and the local time), the channels shown, the owner's note — and the unassigned marks question_resolve writes Set one of the owner's questions' status — investigating, nothing-here, watch, acted (or new) — with its notebook and a note; its marks take the resolution

docs.title: guide
docs.text:
How to investigate with EIS, in one document: the method (one flight first, then across the flights; the mechanism as a hypothesis; alternatives ruled out; what it means and what to do; no verdict words without their reference), the tool map with every parameter form and an example, the notebook rules, this aircraft's record and the owner's notes, its documents, and the workspace in use (flights, date span, open inbox candidates). Call it at the start of every conversation.

No parameters.

docs.title: workspaces_list
docs.text:
The aircraft's workspaces (and any other aircraft's), with the one these tools use. Usually one: the server opens the aircraft's workspace without asking.

No parameters.

docs.title: workspace_use
docs.text:
Writes.

Use another of the aircraft's workspaces for the rest of this conversation (not the EIS pages). Example: {"workspace_id": "ws_2b59350ca5ac"} or the workspace's name.

Parameter Type workspace_id string required

docs.title: flights_list
docs.text:
The workspace's flights, oldest first: local date and start/end time with the zone, route (airports resolved from GPS), takeoffs and landings, the pilot's name, engine hours, source (G3X or AXIS), flight facts, minutes per phase and event count. Filters: date_from/date_to (local YYYY-MM-DD), source, airport (any airport on the route), name (words in the pilot's name or notes), hours_min/hours_max; 50 per page. Example: {"airport": "KBLI", "date_from": "2026-10-01"}.

Parameter Type date_from string Local date YYYY-MM-DD date_to string Local date YYYY-MM-DD source G3X | AXIS airport string An airport code on the route, e.g. KBLI name string Words in the flight's name or notes hours_min number hours_max number offset integer (minimum 0) First row (default 0) limit integer (minimum 1, maximum 50) Rows (≤ 50)

docs.title: flights_find
docs.text:
Flights for a description in words, best first (at most 10), each with what matched: dates ("Oct 24", "2026-10-24", "last Friday", a month or weekday), airports by code or name ("KBLI", "Bellingham"), counts ("three landings", "two stops", "touch and go"), words of the pilot's flight name. Example: {"description": "the Oct 24 flight with three landings, Bellingham"}.

Parameter Type description string required limit integer (minimum 1, maximum 10)

docs.title: flight_get
docs.text:
One flight: header, phases, flight facts, events (limit exceedances and CAS) and the topic findings the Flight view shows. Example: {"flight_id": "1e10d971bd5da136"}.

Parameter Type flight_id string required

docs.title: series_get
docs.text:
Channels of one flight over a window (seconds from the log's start). At most 6 channels; a window of up to 600 s comes back at every row, a longer one as a 600-point min/max envelope per channel. Without a window it answers only for a flight that short. Example: {"flight_id": "1e10d971bd5da136", "channels": ["rpm", "map_inhg"], "start_s": 600, "end_s": 660}.

Parameter Type flight_id string required channels list of string required start_s number end_s number

docs.title: fleet_metrics
docs.text:
The Spec 12 per-flight metrics table (one row per flight, ordered by engine hours) with each metric's baseline, trend, outliers and shift; 50 rows per page. Default metrics: all but the limit_* ones. Example: {"metrics": ["cht_max_f", "oil_temp_max_f"], "limit": 20}.

Parameter Type metrics list of string flights list of string offset integer (minimum 0) First row (default 0) limit integer (minimum 1, maximum 50) Rows (≤ 50)

docs.title: trends_summary
docs.text:
The Trends change summary (ranked metrics with baseline, trend and shift) and the shift history.

No parameters.

docs.title: presets_list
docs.text:
The engine profile's shipped slice rules (Spec 06): id, name, the question each is for, its conditions.

No parameters.

docs.title: slices_build
docs.text:
The slices a selection and slice rules make, each with its local time, context and descriptors; 50 per page. A slice set: flights (default every flight) and slice_rules, each a preset id ("full_power"), a phase ("phase:CLIMB") or a rule object ({"rule_id": "high_map", "name": "MAP >= 38", "conditions": [{"channel": "map_inhg", "op": ">=", "value": 38}], "min_duration_s": 20}); optional hand_slices ([{"flight": "…", "start_s": 600, "end_s": 660}]) and windows ({"rpm": {"window_s": 8, "lag_s": 5}}). Example: {"slice_rules": ["full_power"], "channels": ["rpm", "map_inhg"]}.

Parameter Type slice_rules list of string or object Slice rules: a preset id (presets_list), "phase:CLIMB", or a Spec 06 §5.1 rule object hand_slices list of object Hand slices: flights list of string Flight ids (default: every flight) channels list of string Channels (default rpm, map_inhg) windows object Per channel {window_s, lag_s} (default: the engine's) offset integer (minimum 0) First row (default 0) limit integer (minimum 1, maximum 50) Rows (≤ 50)

docs.title: samples_get
docs.text: The 1 Hz samples of slices, aligned at an anchor (crossing, start, end, peak:CHANNEL). Refuses more than 6000 values — name slice_ids from slices_build. A slice set: flights (default every flight) and slice_rules, each a preset id ("full_power"), a phase ("phase:CLIMB") or a rule object ({"rule_id": "high_map", "name": "MAP >= 38", "conditions": [{"channel": "map_inhg", "op": ">=", "value": 38}], "min_duration_s": 20}); optional hand_slices ([{"flight": "…", "start_s": 600, "end_s": 660}]) and windows ({"rpm": {"window_s": 8, "lag_s": 5}}). Example: {"slice_rules": ["full_power"], "slice_ids": [""], "channels": ["rpm"], "anchor": "start"}. Parameter Type slice_rules list of string or object Slice rules: a preset id (presets_list), "phase:CLIMB", or a Spec 06 §5.1 rule object hand_slices list of object Hand slices: flights list of string Flight ids (default: every flight) channels list of string Channels (default rpm, map_inhg) windows object Per channel {window_s, lag_s} (default: the engine's) slice_ids list of string anchor string

docs.title: question_run
docs.text:
A Spec 06 test over a slice set — cycling, coupling, groups or unusual — with its finding, magnitude with OM references, caveats and the evidence rows (50 per page). A slice set: flights (default every flight) and slice_rules, each a preset id ("full_power"), a phase ("phase:CLIMB") or a rule object ({"rule_id": "high_map", "name": "MAP >= 38", "conditions": [{"channel": "map_inhg", "op": ">=", "value": 38}], "min_duration_s": 20}); optional hand_slices ([{"flight": "…", "start_s": 600, "end_s": 660}]) and windows ({"rpm": {"window_s": 8, "lag_s": 5}}). groups: params.descriptor is channel.measure ("rpm.swing"); params.split is "source" (short for {"by": "source"}), {"by": "date", "date": "2026-10-01"}, {"by": "da_band"}, {"by": "oat_band", "edges": [5, 20]}, {"by": "engine_hours", "edges": [150]}, {"by": "rule"} or {"by": "flights", "groups": [{"label": "before", "flights": ["…"]}, {"label": "after", "flights": ["…"]}]}. Examples: {"test_id": "cycling", "slice_rules": ["full_power"], "channels": ["rpm"]}; {"test_id": "coupling", "slice_rules": ["full_power"], "channels": ["rpm", "map_inhg"]}; {"test_id": "groups", "slice_rules": ["full_power"], "params": {"descriptor": "rpm.swing", "split": "source"}}; {"test_id": "unusual", "slice_rules": ["full_power"]}.

Parameter Type test_id cycling | coupling | groups | unusual required params object Test parameters (Spec 06 §7) reference string slice_rules list of string or object Slice rules: a preset id (presets_list), "phase:CLIMB", or a Spec 06 §5.1 rule object hand_slices list of object Hand slices: flights list of string Flight ids (default: every flight) channels list of string Channels (default rpm, map_inhg) windows object Per channel {window_s, lag_s} (default: the engine's) offset integer (minimum 0) First row (default 0) limit integer (minimum 1, maximum 50) Rows (≤ 50)

docs.title: signal_analyze
docs.text:
One flight's rolling strips, summarised as the runs where each channel cycles (lit), and a window's descriptors, numbers with OM references and diagnostics (periods, the 5 strongest periodogram peaks, best lag) and caveats. Without a window, the window is derived from where the reference channel cycles. skip_onset_s leaves the window's first seconds out of the descriptors and period (a power change at its start buries the cycle; a caveat suggests a value when it sees one). Example: {"flight_id": "1e10d971bd5da136", "start_s": 600, "end_s": 662, "channels": ["rpm", "map_inhg"], "skip_onset_s": 16}.

Parameter Type flight_id string required channels list of string start_s number end_s number reference string skip_onset_s number (minimum 0) Seconds at the window's start left out of the descriptors (default 0) strips boolean Compute the rolling strips (default true)

docs.title: rows_compare
docs.text: One row per slice, grouped by flight, with deltas to a pinned row; 50 rows per page. A slice set: flights (default every flight) and slice_rules, each a preset id ("full_power"), a phase ("phase:CLIMB") or a rule object ({"rule_id": "high_map", "name": "MAP >= 38", "conditions": [{"channel": "map_inhg", "op": ">=", "value": 38}], "min_duration_s": 20}); optional hand_slices ([{"flight": "…", "start_s": 600, "end_s": 660}]) and windows ({"rpm": {"window_s": 8, "lag_s": 5}}). Example: {"slice_rules": ["full_power"], "pinned": ""}. Parameter Type slice_rules list of string or object Slice rules: a preset id (presets_list), "phase:CLIMB", or a Spec 06 §5.1 rule object hand_slices list of object Hand slices: flights list of string Flight ids (default: every flight) channels list of string Channels (default rpm, map_inhg) windows object Per channel {window_s, lag_s} (default: the engine's) reference string pinned string collapse boolean offset integer (minimum 0) First row (default 0) limit integer (minimum 1, maximum 50) Rows (≤ 50)

docs.title: code_run
docs.text:
Writes.

Run Python on the bench and keep it as a code cell in the notebook study_id (study_create first: every executed cell belongs to a notebook) — appended, or replacing cell_id. The namespace has numpy (np), pandas (pd), scipy, matplotlib (plt) and the eis library, the tools' own code: eis.flights(), eis.find("Oct 24 Bellingham"), eis.load(flight, ["rpm"], start_s, end_s), eis.slices("full_power"), eis.cycling("full_power", "rpm") → Result (.finding, .magnitude, .caveats, .rows, .figure(); print(r) is the §8 text), eis.coupling(rule, ["rpm", "map_inhg"]), eis.groups(rule, "rpm.swing", by="source") or by="date", date="2026-10-01", eis.unusual(rule), eis.signal(flight, start_s, end_s, ["rpm"]), eis.compare(rule), eis.logview(flight, start_s, end_s, ["rpm", "map_inhg"], marks=[(t_s, "label")]), eis.document("om.pdf").find("boost"), eis.aircraft, eis.profile, eis.notes. eis.table(df, caption="…", units={col: unit}) and eis.figure(fig, caption="…") make evidence. role: evidence (one captioned eis.table / eis.figure / eis.logview, no print), support (the calculation behind the evidence after it; the default), scratch (exploring — kept under Working). section: 4 Findings (default), 5 How this was done, 6 Follow-ups, 7 Working. A rule is a preset id, "phase:CLIMB", a rule object or {selection, slice_rules, hand_slices}. Each cell starts afresh: nothing carries over from earlier cells, so load what it needs in it. A cell that fails is fixed by running it again with its cell_id, not by adding another. The last expression's value is shown, as in Jupyter. No network, no subprocesses, writes only under FILES, time and memory capped. Returns stdout (≤ 8000 characters), tables (text) and up to 4 figures as images. Example: {"study_id": "…", "source": "r = eis.cycling('full_power', 'rpm')\nprint(r)"}.

Parameter Type study_id string required source string required cell_id string role evidence | support | scratch section 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 timeout_s number (minimum 1, maximum 300) Default 60 memory_mb number (minimum 256, maximum 8192) Default 2048

docs.title: profile_get
docs.text:
The engine profile: limits with their Operators Manual references.

No parameters.

docs.title: aircraft_get
docs.text:
The aircraft record: name, airframe, engine serial, propeller, controller, firmware, avionics, the documents folders; the owner's notes (notes.md) whole; its workspaces; the engine model and the Settings → Log channels assignments.

No parameters.

docs.title: documents_list
docs.text:
The aircraft's documents — the Operators Manual, service bulletins, manuals, notes — read in place from the folders the owner named (Settings → Aircraft → Documents folders; subfolders included): name, folder, kind, pages, first line. With no folder set it says so.

No parameters.

docs.title: document_read
docs.text:
Pages of one document (at most 3 at a time), or the pages where a phrase occurs (find: case-insensitive, accents ignored, with snippets). Never a whole manual. Examples: {"name": "Bulletins/APL-SB-23.pdf", "find": "hunting"}, {"name": "om.md", "page": 5, "pages": 2}.

Parameter Type name string required page integer (minimum 1) pages integer (minimum 1, maximum 3) find string

docs.title: journal_list
docs.text:
The Journal entries as the UI shows them; 50 per page.

Parameter Type offset integer (minimum 0) First row (default 0) limit integer (minimum 1, maximum 50) Rows (≤ 50)

docs.title: studies_list
docs.text:
The notebooks in the workspace, newest first: kind, author, question, status, finding, and each one's card — origin, channels, flights and dates, evidence, tests, outputs, resolution, tags.

No parameters.

docs.title: study_read
docs.text:
One study: a notebook's metadata (question, status, summary) and its cells with their outputs (figures named, not drawn; pending re-run outputs flagged).

Parameter Type study_id string required

docs.title: study_create
docs.text:
Writes.

Start an investigation notebook for a question; its first cell holds the question. Add cells with cell_append and code_run, end with study_finish. With question_id (one of the owner's questions, pins_list) the notebook opens with the owner's marks: each mark's note, then a log view of its window. Example: {"name": "Full-power rpm cycling", "question": "Why does rpm hunt at full power?"}, or {"name": "Rough climbs", "question_id": "q-1a2b3c4d"}.

Parameter Type name string required question string kind investigation | question-for-type inbox_candidate string The inbox candidate this investigates (marked investigating) question_id string The owner's question this takes up (pins_list): marked investigating, and a markdown cell with each mark's note followed by its log view engine_type string

docs.title: cell_append
docs.text:
Writes.

Append a cell to a notebook, at the end of its section: markdown (source) — a finding's one sentence, what a result means, the plan; code (source, run at once, as code_run); logview (flight, start_s, end_s, channels, marks [[t_s, "label"], …], title, caption) — a strip chart of a window of one flight that the EIS pages open as the Flight view (evidence by default). role: markdown narrative (default) or scratch; code evidence, support (default) or scratch. section: 4 Findings (default; the open follow-up when there is one), 5 How this was done, 6 Follow-ups, 7 Working (scratch goes there). Example: {"kind": "logview", "flight": "…", "start_s": 360, "end_s": 420, "channels": ["rpm", "map_inhg"], "marks": [[367, "takeoff power"]]}.

Parameter Type study_id string required kind markdown | code | logview required source string role evidence | support | scratch | narrative section 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 flight string start_s number end_s number channels list of string marks list of list of values title string caption string rule string timeout_s number memory_mb number

docs.title: study_rerun
docs.text:
Writes.

Re-run every code cell of a notebook against this workspace; outputs that differ wait as pending until study_accept or study_discard.

Parameter Type study_id string required

docs.title: study_accept
docs.text:
Writes.

Accept the pending re-run outputs (all, or cell_ids): they become the cells' outputs. With source "external": accept instead the outputs a kernel outside EIS (JupyterLab) saved in the notebook, as they stand (cells marked ran elsewhere). Example: {"study_id": "…", "cell_ids": ["c6"]}.

Parameter Type study_id string required cell_ids list of string source rerun | external rerun (default): the bench's pending outputs; external: outputs saved outside EIS

docs.title: study_discard
docs.text:
Writes.

Discard the pending re-run outputs (all, or cell_ids); the stored outputs stand. Example: {"study_id": "…", "cell_ids": ["c6"]}.

Parameter Type study_id string required cell_ids list of string

docs.title: study_finish
docs.text:
Writes.

End an investigation with its Answer, which EIS writes as sections 1–3: question_scope (the flights and dates looked at, the references used, what was taken as given, what the logs can't tell — a short list), shows (3–5 sentences, each a number the data shows; shows[0] is the Journal's line), means (the hypothesis, confidence in words, what would change the view), actions ([{what, who, settles, recheck_after_flights?}], or [] with actions_none saying why). summary alone still finishes. With a follow-up open, changed: what changed above. Scratch cells move under Working. Refused, naming the cells, while a figure or log view has nothing saying what it shows, a code cell ends in an error, an evidence cell shows plain text, or a support cell has nothing after it. Optionally resolves its inbox candidate, resolves the owner's question it answered (question; with its marks; resolution defaults to watch for a question) and notes the finding in the Journal (the one Journal entry Claude may write). finding: one sentence, what was found — the Journal's line under the notebook's title (shows[0] when shows is given; else the note, else the summary's first sentence). tags: two or three topic words for the notebook's card on Research home — what it is about, not what it found. Reports the flights the cells read and the inbox's open candidates. Example: {"study_id": "…", "summary": "…", "question": "q-1a2b3c4d", "resolution": "watch", "tags": ["governor", "cruise rpm"], "journal": true, "question_scope": "- 63 flights, Mar–Nov 2026\n- OM Ed. 0 Rev. 1 p. 30 limits", "shows": ["RPM swings 180 rpm at full power on 94 of 100 slices (Table 1)."], "means": "…", "actions": [{"what": "Ask the shop to check the governor", "who": "A&P", "settles": "whether the governor is the cause", "recheck_after_flights": 10}]}.

Parameter Type study_id string required summary string inbox_candidate string question string The owner's question this answers (pins_list); it and its marks take the resolution resolution investigating | nothing-here | watch | acted note string journal boolean finding string One sentence, what was found: the Journal's line (at most 240 characters) tags list of string Two or three topic words (at most 5): what the notebook is about question_scope string Scope and qualifications: flights and dates, references, what was taken as given, what the logs can't tell shows list of string What the data shows: 3–5 sentences with numbers, each pointing at its evidence means string What it means: the hypothesis, confidence in words, what would change the view actions list of object Proposed actions; [] with actions_none when there are none actions_none string Why there is nothing to do (with actions: []) changed string With a follow-up open: what changed above (the Answer, the actions)

docs.title: study_followup
docs.text:
Writes.

Open a dated follow-up in a notebook (section 6): later cells appended without a section land in it, and study_finish closes it with changed — what changed above. New analysis in a finished notebook opens one itself, dated today. Example: {"study_id": "…", "date": "2026-11-27", "title": "Is phase a factor?"}.

Parameter Type study_id string required date string YYYY-MM-DD (default today) title string

docs.title: cell_edit
docs.text:
Writes.

Change a cell's role (code: evidence, support, scratch; markdown: narrative, scratch), move it to the end of a section (4 Findings, 5 How this was done, 6 Follow-ups, 7 Working), or replace a markdown cell's text. Code changes with code_run and its cell_id, so it runs. Sections 1–3 are study_finish's. Example: {"study_id": "…", "cell_id": "c3", "role": "scratch"} or {"study_id": "…", "cell_id": "c19", "section": 5}.

Parameter Type study_id string required cell_id string required role evidence | support | scratch | narrative section 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 source string

docs.title: inbox_list
docs.text:
The candidates the detectors raised (recurring patterns, stand-out flights, shifts, groups) with evidence and status; scans first when there are new flights. Example: {"status": ["new", "investigating"]}.

Parameter Type status string or list of string

docs.title: inbox_resolve
docs.text:
Writes.

Set a candidate's status — investigating, nothing-here, watch, acted (or new) — with its study and a note. Example: {"candidate_id": "…", "status": "nothing-here", "note": "the governor, known"}.

Parameter Type candidate_id string required status new | investigating | nothing-here | watch | acted required study_id string note string

docs.title: pins_list
docs.text:
The owner's questions and marks (Mark for Claude on the Flight view): each question with its status, notebook and marks — flight, window (start_s, end_s and the local time), the channels shown, the owner's note — and the unassigned marks. A mark is where to look and a sentence, not a finding. newest_open names the question to take up when the owner asks without saying which. Example: {"status": ["new", "investigating"]}.

Parameter Type status string or list of string

docs.title: question_resolve
docs.text:
Writes.

Set one of the owner's questions' status — investigating, nothing-here, watch, acted (or new) — with its notebook and a note; its marks take the resolution. study_finish with question does this as it ends a notebook. Example: {"question_id": "q-1a2b3c4d", "status": "watch", "study_id": "st-…"}.

Parameter Type question_id string required status new | investigating | nothing-here | watch | acted required study_id string note string

docs.title: The notebook format
docs.text: An investigation is a standard Jupyter notebook (nbformat 4) — it opens in JupyterLab, VS Code or anything that reads .ipynb — with a few EIS fields in places the format reserves for tools. Spec 16 §5.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
<data folder>/workspaces/<workspace id>/studies/<study id>/
    notebook.ipynb
    files/              anything a cell wrote (figures, tables), referenced relatively

Export notebook (.zip) is that folder. Flights are named by fingerprint in an export (src:…, derived from each log, meaningless without the same file), so a notebook travels without your logs; importing it maps the fingerprints back to the importer's flights, and cells whose flights aren't there are read-only.

docs.title: The notebook's metadata
docs.text:
metadata.slingology:

Field id, name the study's id and title kind investigation, or question-for-type (a question for every owner of the engine type) author claude or user question the question as asked status, summary open or finished; the summary written at the finish (What it means, or the older free-text summary) shape 1 for a notebook laid out in the seven sections (The shape); absent on older notebooks top the structured Answer of the last finish: question_scope, shows (3–5 sentences), means, actions (what, who, settles, recheck_after_flights) or actions_none history each earlier top, with the date it was replaced (finished) finding shows[0] — the notebook's line in the Journal followup the follow-up open now, if any (its heading cell's id) card the Research home card: origin, channels, flights, dates, evidence counts, tests, outputs, tags, actions inbox_candidate the inbox candidate it investigates, if any engine, engine_type the EIS engine version that wrote it; the engine model created, updated, finished times (UTC) imported, converted_from where it came from, when it did

docs.title: Cells
docs.text:
Standard markdown and code cells. The first code cell is the setup cell (id setup), which binds eis to the workspace (the eis library). Every cell has a metadata.slingology.role (Cell roles). Each code cell carries metadata.slingology.ran:

Field engine the engine version it ran on flights the flights its output depends on (ids here; fingerprints once exported) at, ms, status when, how long, and whether it ran to the end

A cell whose outputs were saved by a kernel outside EIS (JupyterLab, say) no longer matches its ran: EIS shows it ran elsewhere until it is re-run on the bench or its outputs are kept as they are.

After Re-run, a code cell whose output changed holds the new outputs in metadata.slingology.pending, beside the stored outputs, until they are accepted or discarded.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Standard nbformat outputs: stream (printed text), and execute_result / display_data with text/plain, text/html (tables) and image/svg+xml (figures).

A log view is one output with two representations:

MIME type Holds image/svg+xml the strip chart, drawn — what Jupyter, the exported page and a PDF show application/vnd.slingology.logview+json a reference, never samples: flight, flight_date_local, start_s, end_s, channels, marks ({t_s, label}), title, window_label, rule

The EIS pages read the reference and show the Flight view's chart for that window, with Open flight. If the flight isn't in the workspace they show the picture, marked Flight not in this workspace.

An evidence output — what eis.table, eis.figure and eis.logview(…, caption=) produce — carries metadata.slingology.evidence: kind (table, figure, logview), caption, and for a table its units; a table also carries slingology.table (n_rows, n_cols, truncated). The number (Table 1) is the renderer's, counted in order, so moving a cell never leaves a stale number.

docs.title: The shape
docs.text:
A notebook is laid out in seven sections, in this order. study_create writes their headings — markdown cells with role section, ids s1–s7. Spec 16 §5.6.

Section Holds Written by 1 The question the question; Scope and qualifications the finish (question_scope) 2 Answer What the data shows (3–5 bullets); What it means the finish (shows, means) 3 Proposed actions numbered: what · who · what it would settle · re-check after the next N flights — or None, and why the finish (actions) 4 Findings each finding: one sentence, then its evidence cell (and the calculation behind it) Claude 5 How this was done the plan, the data and slice rules in words, the method, alternatives ruled out, outside context labelled as context Claude 6 Follow-ups dated subsections (### Follow-up — 2026-11-27: title), each ending with what changed above Claude, after study_followup 7 Working every scratch cell, in the order written gathered at the finish

Sections 1–3 are written from the finish's fields, not from markdown: the .ipynb holds them as markdown cells marked generated: true, so JupyterLab shows the same text, and a re-finish rewrites them and keeps the earlier Answer in history. A follow-up opens when Claude asks for one, or by itself when new analysis lands in a finished notebook.

docs.title: Cell roles
docs.text:
Role Cell evidence code a table, figure or log view the reader reads without the code — shown open, numbered, with its caption support code the computation behind the evidence or sentence after it — folded under show the calculation. A code cell without a role is support scratch code or markdown exploring — kept, folded, under Working narrative markdown a finding's sentence, what a result means, the plan. A markdown cell without a role is narrative section, followup, changed, setup — written by EIS: the headings, a follow-up's heading and its What changed above line, the setup cell

Older notebooks (no shape) get roles when first loaded — code cells support, markdown narrative — and nothing moves; they render as before. Moving any cell into a section gives the notebook its seven headings, with its cells under Findings.

docs.title: The finish rule
docs.text:
study_finish takes the Answer as fields — question_scope, shows, means, actions (or actions_none), and changed when a follow-up is open; a summary alone is still accepted and stands as What it means. It refuses, naming the cells, while:

  • a figure or log view has nothing saying what it shows — a caption, or a markdown cell right before or after it;
  • a code cell ends in an error;
  • an evidence cell's output is plain printed text;
  • a support cell has nothing after it — no evidence and no sentence that uses it.

A notebook says what each picture means, and a cell that failed is replaced, not left behind a working copy. Each code cell starts afresh, so it loads what it uses itself; when one fails on a name an earlier cell set, its error says which cell that was. At the finish the scratch cells move under Working.

docs.title: The two renderings
docs.text: The Research page and Export as a page (.html) use the same renderer — the page on the website and on your computer show the same notebook — and both pass tables through a filter that keeps only plain table markup. A shaped notebook reads as its sections: 1–3 typeset as one block (earlier Answers folded inside it), each finding's evidence open with its number and caption and the calculation folded beside it, then How this was done, the dated follow-ups, and Working (n cells) folded at the end. The Research home card says n actions.

docs.title: The research paper
docs.text:
About this page

This is the project's research paper, published here unchanged from docs/ROTAX 91XiS Engine Data Analytics.md in the repository. It is written for readers who want the evidence and reasoning behind the app; the concept pages say the same things in plain language.

docs.title: A Research Foundation for FADEC-Native Engine Monitoring
docs.text:
Slingology EIS Project | N117ZS Sling TSi | KAWO

Living Document — Edition 0.4 (draft for review) | October 2026

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text:
This paper documents a research programme to build open-source, FADEC-native engine health analytics for Rotax iS-powered aircraft, and records what the first 58 flights of one Rotax 916iS have shown. General-purpose platforms such as Savvy Aviation and FlySto are built around pilot-controlled mixture management; their signature diagnostics (rich-of-peak / lean-of-peak analysis, exhaust-valve detection from leaning behaviour) do not apply to an engine whose dual-lane ECU sets fuel, spark and operating mode itself. SlingologyEIS starts instead from what the iS engine actually controls and what its Garmin engine log actually contains.

Since Edition 0.3 the toolkit has become an application. SlingologyEIS 1.0.1 (October 2026) runs either as a local server or entirely inside the browser, reads Garmin G3X, Garmin Pilot and Garmin AXIS logs, keeps per-aircraft workspaces whose logs never leave the pilot's own folders, and answers two questions about every flight: did anything go outside the Rotax Operators Manual limits (events), and is this flight unusual for this engine (insights against a reference learned only from the aircraft's own history). A Trends page asks the second question over a longer horizon — is my engine changing. The analytics topics shown to pilots now rest on written admission criteria; several of Edition 0.3's modules were removed or demoted under them, and one of its findings — four "in-flight" ENGINE ECU events — was withdrawn as a classifier defect.

The dataset is 120 logs from N117ZS (April–October 2026, engine hours 28.2 → 122.2): 59 ground sessions are skipped automatically and three duplicate exports collapse, leaving 58 flights and 76 airborne hours. Findings as of this edition: cylinder 4 is the hottest cylinder on 58/58 flights, by a median 40 °F; cruise EGT spread averages 60.3 ± 5.5 °F and is rising at 0.12 °F per engine hour (R² 0.42), with the last twelve flights 5 °F wider than the reference, carried by cylinder 4; oil and coolant peaks have never approached their limits (201 ± 12 °F and 181 ± 7 °F against 248 °F) and depend on flight length more than on weather; one time-at-takeoff-power exceedance (389 s against 300 s) and one close call; the takeoff manifold-pressure model now stands at n = 56, R² 0.64, with the recent takeoffs delivering about 0.8 inHg more boost than it predicts; zero in-flight ENGINE ECU events in 117 logs. Three Operators Manual limits fire on most flights for diagnosed aircraft-specific reasons (fuel-pressure sender offset, a low idle setting, propeller-governor overshoot) and are handled by filters with a note rather than by changing the limits.

The long-term goal is unchanged: free, FADEC-native engine monitoring for the Rotax iS community, validated beyond a single aircraft.

docs.title: 1. Introduction and Motivation
docs.text:
The Rotax 916iS is a turbocharged, intercooled, liquid-cooled-head, FADEC-controlled four-cylinder engine: 160 hp (119 kW) at takeoff, 2,000-hour TBO, the highest-performance engine in the Rotax light-aviation line. The 915iS (139 hp, turbocharged) and 912iS (100 hp, normally aspirated) share its control architecture. All three differ from the Lycoming and Continental engines that dominate general-aviation analytics tooling in three ways that matter for engine monitoring:

  • No pilot mixture control. A dual-redundant ECU (Lane A / Lane B) reads throttle position, manifold pressure and air temperature and from them sets injection, ignition timing and — above roughly 97 % throttle — the ECO/POWER mode transition. The pilot has one input, the throttle.
  • Liquid-cooled cylinder heads, air-cooled barrels. The cooling-health observables are coolant temperature and EGT, not cylinder-head temperature in the traditional sense.
  • FADEC-calculated fuel flow. There is no physical flow sensor. Fuel flow is a model-based value with a manufacturer-stated tolerance of about ±10 %.

Existing platforms do not account for this. Savvy Aviation's FEVA exhaust-valve analytics and ROP/LOP diagnostics depend on the mixture being varied by hand; on a FADEC engine they either cannot run or produce noise. FlySto replays flights and graphs any channel but has no engine-health model for an iS engine. Rotax's own B.U.D.S. software reads the ECU fault log directly but needs a hardware interface and is used at maintenance, not after every flight. A pilot with a Rotax iS engine and a modern glass panel has therefore been collecting a rich engine log on every flight with nothing designed to read it.

The question this programme asks is: with the mixture fixed by the computer, which engine-health questions can a flight log answer, and how should they be answered so that a pilot can trust them? The answers so far are the subject of this paper.

What changed since Edition 0.3. Edition 0.3 (July 2026) described a Python toolkit and a 23-flight dataset. Since then: the dataset has grown to 58 flights; the toolkit has become a web application with a local-server and an in-browser mode; the aircraft's avionics changed from Garmin G3X to Garmin AXIS, adding a second log format; the analytics topics were audited against written admission criteria and the set changed; limit detection was reworked after a diagnosis of why some limits fired on every flight; limit filters, a change monitor, a Trends change page and a Journal of decisions were added; and the ENGINE ECU finding of Edition 0.3 was corrected. Each of these is covered below.

docs.title: 2.1 Garmin EIS log sources
docs.text:
The engine reads Garmin engine logs from three export paths. All three normalise, inside the loader, to one channel registry; nothing downstream knows which path produced a frame.

Source Identification Layout Sampling Notes G3X direct (GDU 460 + GEA-24) Row 1 #airframe_info … product="GDU 4xx" metadata row · column header · 1 Hz rows 1 Hz (verified: all inter-row deltas 1.000 s, N = 16,198) Primary source April–October 2026. File name log_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_ICAO.csv; 111 columns. Garmin Pilot export As above with row 2 prefixed # same 1 Hz Same columns; any file name. A flight exported both ways appears twice and collapses to one (§2.4). Garmin AXIS Row 1 Product="AXIS"; row 2 a # units row; row 3 camelCase column names metadata · units · column names · rows ≈ 0.83 Hz Since October 2026 on N117ZS. Variable column set — 102 columns on one log, 117 on the next; mapping is by name only.

The G3X metadata row carries aircraft ident, software version, system ID, airframe hours and engine hours. The AXIS carries the ident as tail_number, no system ID and no hours fields; engine hours are taken from the first row's e1TachTime channel — on N117ZS the same hour meter the G3X wrote (119.6 h on 14 October 2026, continuous with the G3X series), so baselines and trends carry straight across the avionics change with no user input.

AXIS sampling. The AXIS writes roughly five samples every six seconds (a repeating pattern of four 1,000 ms steps and one 2,000 ms step), so about one row in six is missing. Several engine paths count rows as seconds. The loader therefore reindexes AXIS frames onto a 1-second grid: numeric channels are linearly interpolated across holes of at most 2 s, text and CAS channels carry the previous value forward, longer holes stay missing, filled rows are flagged, and every AXIS analysis carries an informational diagnostic with the filled share (≈ 17 %). G3X logs are never resampled. G3X and AXIS frames are therefore sample-for-sample comparable, and phase detection, limits and topics produce the same classes on either. A time-based engine (elapsed-second arithmetic throughout) is the honest long-term fix and is on the backlog as hardening.

AXIS differences handled in the loader. CAS alert tokens are normalised to the G3X wording through a per-source alias table (EFIS ON BACKUP → EFIS ON BKUP, NAV ON BACKUP → NAV ON BKUP), so events, filters and Journal entries use one name per alert; AXIS names the ECU alert ENGINE ECU as the G3X does (confirmed on the 18 October log). General-purpose analog inputs (engine1GeneralPurposeAnalog<n>) carry whatever the installation wired to them and are never mapped by assumption: they enter under a raw id and appear under a registry name (CO ppm on N117ZS) only when the pilot assigns them in the app's settings. AXIS-only channels (onGroundState, flightTime, e1TachTime) are carried raw and are not used by phase detection, so a reference built from G3X flights stays valid for AXIS flights of the same aircraft. The first AXIS logs examined opened with the engine already running, one to two minutes after boot; of the five now in the set, two do record the engine start, three carry a complete two-lane check, and all five name the alert ENGINE ECU (§8) — so the ECU classifier works unchanged on AXIS, and a log that opens mid-run is treated as normal for the source rather than as a mid-log power cycle.

docs.title: 2.2 Engine parameters available from the FADEC CAN bus
docs.text:
The GEA-24 (and the AXIS engine interface) receives the following from the 916iS over the Rotax display CAN bus (Garmin G3X Installation Manual §24.2.2.3; Rotax OM communication-interfaces section):

Channel Source Notes RPM FADEC CAN Propeller-shaft rpm after gearbox reduction Engine power (%) FADEC CAN ECU-computed share of rated power; can exceed 100 % at takeoff Manifold pressure (inHg) FADEC CAN Plenum pressure; the turbocharger health observable Oil pressure (psi), oil temperature (°F) FADEC CAN Coolant temperature (°F) FADEC CAN Cylinder-head liquid cooling Fuel flow (gal/h) FADEC calculated Model-based; no physical sensor; ±10 % Fuel pressure (psi) Separate sensor Rail pressure relative to manifold pressure EGT1–4 (°F) FADEC CAN Per-cylinder exhaust gas temperature Main volts, battery amps GEA-24 / AXIS Bus voltage and battery current CAS alert string Avionics Composite annunciation of all active alerts (ENGINE ECU, FUEL PRESS, OIL PRESS, …)

Plus the flight data the analytics need to know what the aircraft was doing: indicated and true airspeed, ground speed, barometric and GPS altitude, vertical speed, outside air temperature, density altitude, position.

docs.title: 2.3 Parameters not available in the log
docs.text:
The following exist in the ECU but are not exposed over the display CAN bus and do not appear in any of the three log formats. They are accessible only through B.U.D.S. at maintenance:

  • Throttle position — the quantity that determines ECO vs POWER mode
  • Lane A / Lane B individual fault codes and status
  • Injector pulse width per cylinder; ignition advance angle
  • Wastegate (boost-control valve) position
  • Manifold air temperature (on the CAN bus, not in the standard column set)
  • The ECU's internal fault history

This gap is a design constraint, not a footnote. The topic-admission criteria (§7.1) exclude any topic that needs one of these channels, and the app never infers them. ECO/POWER mode detection remains an open research item (§4).

docs.title: 2.4 The dataset
docs.text:
Aircraft N117ZS, Sling TSi, Rotax 916iS, constant-speed propeller with governor Avionics Garmin G3X Touch (GDU 460, GEA-24) to 5 October 2026; Garmin AXIS from 14 October 2026 Logs 120 files: 112 G3X direct, 3 Garmin Pilot exports, 5 AXIS Admission 59 ground sessions skipped (no airborne phase); 3 duplicate exports collapsed; 0 short flights; 0 corrupt logs → 58 flights (52 G3X, 1 Garmin Pilot, 5 AXIS) Period 8 April – 18 October 2026; engine hours 28.2 → 122.2 Time 93.9 h recorded, 76.0 h airborne; median flight 45 min airborne, longest 293 min; 17 flights under 20 min airborne, 26 over an hour Departures 18 airports; home field KAWO (27 departures); a July cross-country to Oshkosh (KBIL, KFCM, KOSH, KMML, KRAP, KHLN); 5 departures above 2,000 ft pressure altitude (max 3,685 ft, KHLN) Conditions cruise OAT 1.6–24.1 °C (OAT bands: 48 mild, 6 cold, 1 warm, 0 hot; 3 flights with no cruise); cruise density altitude 775–15,506 ft (DA bands: 12 low, 28 moderate, 7 high, 8 very high); maximum altitude 15,066 ft Fuel 508 gal FADEC-integrated, 6.7 gal per airborne hour overall

The same 120 logs are the test set for the application: the characterization and contract tests assert on this set's counts, and every analysis in this paper was produced by the released engine (1.0.1) with its shipped defaults and no filters applied — the topics' natural signal, not what the pilot sees after setting filters.

Single-aircraft caveat. Every empirical number in this paper comes from one 916iS in one airframe. The topic register records every such finding as E3 (916iS, 1 aircraft), and every topic is Unverified on the 912iS and 915iS until data from such an aircraft exists (§7.1).

docs.title: 3. Operating Limits and How They Become Events
3.1 Engine profiles
docs.text:
Limits come from each engine's Rotax Operators Manual and live in an engine profile (engines/<model>.json) with the edition cited. The OM text is never stored in the repository.

A "914iS" placeholder that existed earlier was removed: the Rotax 914 is a carburetted turbo engine, not an iS engine, and no such OM exists.
