Remote support/configuration session with Airmaster to be scheduled; diagnostic test flight superseded by a before/after comparison. No airworthiness action taken (see §6).

Change log - 2026-10-29 — Initial write-up after analysis of 98 takeoffs (Apr 8 – Oct 28 2026) and Rotax OM-916 i A/C24 Ed0 Rev1. - 2026-10-29 (rev 3) — Email sent to Airmaster (configuration, symptom, example plot, 94/98 figure). Same-day reply: "known behaviour" on the 916iS; firmware updates for controller and hub address the TO-mode hunting, "still having teething problems with some customers but the severity is much less"; Airmaster now performs the updates and diagnostics download by remote session into the customer's PC rather than sending instructions. Reply sent proposing Pacific afternoon slots and asking what to have ready (Windows laptop, A0117 cable on CN4, aircraft power) and which versions will be installed. - 2026-10-29 (rev 2) — Propeller logbook reviewed: controller is AC300F and the Take-Off preset is 5700, not 5800. Mean rpm in every takeoff (5705–5715) matches that setpoint. Test plan revised: Hold steps at 5600/5550/5500 instead of 5700; Manual test unchanged.

docs.title: 1. Symptom
docs.text:
With the Airmaster controller in Takeoff mode (preset 5700 rpm) and wide-open throttle, engine rpm does not hold steady. It cycles by roughly ±90 rpm around the 5700 setpoint with a period of 4–5 s, and manifold pressure cycles with it between ~45 and ~50 inHg. Fuel flow follows one second behind. Power varies roughly ±6% per cycle. The oscillation begins the moment rpm passes ~5600 (at rotation on a normal takeoff; within 2 s on a touch-and-go) and stops the moment Climb mode (5400 rpm) is selected, with throttle unchanged. Climb and Cruise modes are steady.

First noticed by the pilot on 2026-10-24 during a touch-and-go at KBLI, as a fore-aft surge felt in the climb in calm air.

docs.title: 2.1 Sources
docs.text:
• 121 CSV logs from the owner’s log set (the flights dated through 2026-10-28): Garmin G3X Touch (GDU 460, 1 Hz) from 2026-04-08 (28 engine hours, Phase 1 at KTOA) through 2026-10-05, and Garmin AXIS (1 Hz) from 2026-10-14 through 2026-10-28.
  • Every segment with rpm ≥ 5550 for ≥ 15 s was extracted (98 distinct segments after removing duplicate files). Metrics per segment: rpm and MAP min/max, median 12-second rpm peak-to-peak ("swing"), period (peak counting), rpm–MAP correlation, OAT, pressure and density altitude, wind, vertical-g scatter.
  • 46 logs contained no full-power segment (taxi/ground runs, partial exports); 14 were startup-only fragments.

docs.title: 2.2 Headline result
docs.text:
94 of 98 takeoffs oscillate. Median swing 180 rpm (range 140–240), period 4.4 s (IQR 4.1–4.8). Amplitude and period are the same in April (28–33 hr) as in October (145 hr), and the same on G3X and AXIS logs. Nothing has drifted; this is a structural characteristic of the installation from delivery.

DA band takeoffs median rpm swing typical MAP peak < 3000 ft 92 180 rpm 49–50 inHg 3500–4900 ft (KACV, KSFF, KRAP) 3 125–140 rpm ("weak") 49.9 6000–6350 ft (KBIL, KHLN) 2 70–80 rpm (clean) 51.4–51.5
  • Amplitude vs density altitude: r = −0.50 (monotonic decline above ~3500 ft DA).
  • Amplitude vs OAT at a given DA: r = 0.05 (no effect). Amplitude vs turbulence (vertical-g scatter): no effect.
  • Rpm–MAP correlation at zero lag: 0.89–0.97 on AXIS logs; 0.1–0.3 on G3X logs. The G3X appears to damp its MAP channel (2 inHg ripple vs 5–7 inHg on AXIS for the same oscillation); rpm amplitude is identical on both, so the G3X MAP traces are treated as smoothed.
  • Ground roll is clean on normal takeoffs (5520–5550 rpm, MAP 42.5–43, prop on fine-pitch stop); oscillation starts when rpm passes ~5600.
  • Climb mode at WOT: 12-s rpm ripple 20–75 rpm, MAP ripple 0.1–0.9 inHg, in every log checked.

docs.title: 2.3 Example: 2026-10-24, three takeoffs (AXIS)
docs.text:
Takeoff rpm swing MAP range period OAT / PA KAWO 15:26 ~±110 43.4–50.0 3.7 s 5 °C / −150 ft KPAE 15:51 ~±100 43.4–49.9 4.3 s 6 °C / 1430 ft KBLI T&G 16:22 ~±100 44.4–49.9 4.0 s 5 °C / 2380 ft

Longitudinal acceleration correlates with rpm at zero lag (0.42 / 0.33 / 0.52). The KBLI event was felt because the air was calmest (vertical-g σ 0.050 vs 0.063 / 0.077; wind 5 kt vs 11–13 kt), not because the oscillation was larger.

docs.title: 3. Mechanism
docs.text:
Two correctly-functioning controllers are coupled through the 916iS boost schedule.

Rotax side (OM-916 i A/C24, Ed0 Rev1). Chapter 5 engine deck, WOT, sea level, ISA:

rpm p_plenum power 5000 1409 mbar (41.6 inHg) 92.8 kW 5500 1484 mbar (43.8 inHg) 104.7 kW 5800 1722 mbar (50.8 inHg) 119.0 kW

The boost target rises 75 mbar from 5000 to 5500 rpm and 238 mbar from 5500 to 5800: the entire takeoff boost increment, and a 14% power step, is scheduled inside the last 300 rpm. §2.1 states the same targets (1480 mbar at 5500, 1690 at 5800, 25–35 °C). The logged data sits exactly on this curve: across one cycle the plenum pressure moves between ~1520 and ~1690 mbar as rpm swings about the setpoint. The ECU is doing what the manual says.

Airmaster side. The AC300F governs rpm by driving blade pitch with an electric actuator through a digital control loop; the operator's manual describes a non-linear response with software-set parameters and a governing band of roughly ±100 rpm. It is inherently slower than a hydraulic governor.

The loop. Rpm droops slightly → ECU lowers the boost target (wastegate opens) → power falls → rpm droops further → governor fines pitch → rpm rises past the setpoint → ECU raises boost → power rises → rpm rises further. Turbo spool lag on one side and actuator lag on the other give a natural period of ~4.4 s. In Climb mode (5400 rpm) the boost target is nearly flat with rpm, so there is nothing to feed back and the governor holds steady. Note that the setpoint is already 100 rpm below the engine limit — the usual "set TO to 5700" advice for Airmaster/Rotax installations is already applied and does not prevent the loop.

Hot-and-high exceptions. The engine deck shows the same ramp at 3000 and 6000 ft, so the ramp does not disappear with altitude. At KBIL and KHLN (DA ~6000–6350 ft) MAP sat flat at 51.4–51.5 inHg (~1744 mbar), at the 1750 mbar "not to exceed" value the OM says the boost control uses. With boost pinned at its ceiling it no longer varies with rpm, the feedback path is open, and only ordinary governing ripple remains. (A contributing factor may be the prop sitting closer to its fine-pitch stop at altitude, reducing governor authority.)

Attribution. The boost ramp is universal to every 916iS; the overwhelming majority of 916 TSis fly MT hydraulic governors and show no reported hunting, and Rotax certified the engine against a hydraulic governor. The variable is governor response. This is therefore an Airmaster tuning question for the AP431/AC200 on the 916iS, not an engine fault — and not an Airmaster defect either, but a combination neither party appears to have tested for. The AP431 for the 916 shipped in 2025; N117ZS is one of the earliest installs.

docs.title: 4. Hypotheses considered and eliminated
docs.text:
• Governor hunting alone (constant boost): no — MAP swings 5–7 inHg in lockstep with rpm.
  • ECU speed-limiter intervention: no — no fuel/EGT signature; the oscillation starts at 5600, well below the limit, and its amplitude is set by the governor, not clipped by the limiter.
  • Overload clutch slip (SB-916i-003 signature: spike to 6500 then dip to 4000): no — wrong waveform.
  • Touch-and-go / boost-transient specific: no — present on every normal takeoff.
  • Slipring/brush/actuator wear: no — amplitude identical from 28 hr to 145 hr. (Slipring inspection still worth doing at next opportunity per Airmaster schedule, 145 hr with none recorded.)
  • Turbulence or OAT: no correlation.
  • Display artifact: no — identical rpm amplitude on G3X and AXIS.

docs.title: 5. Why it went unnoticed for 145 hours
docs.text: Onset is at rotation, when attention is outside; it ends at the Climb selection ~40 s later. The G3X damped engine data and a ±90 rpm needle movement on a 6000-rpm arc is not conspicuous; the AXIS shows raw CAN values. The surge is ~0.04 g, which is masked by light chop and only stands out in calm air. A TAF test pilot, the CFI, and the owner all flew behind it without noticing; nobody missed anything obvious.

docs.title: 6. Limits status (OM-916 i A/C24 §2.1, §3.5)
docs.text:
• Manifold pressure: limit 1800 hPa (53.15 inHg); boost-control "not to exceed" 1750 mbar. Logged maximum 51.5 inHg (~1744 mbar). Inside limits.
  • Engine speed: limit 5800 rpm (max 5 min). Governor setpoint 5700, 100 rpm below the limit; the cycle is a swing about that setpoint. Logged values were reviewed against the OM §3.5 exceedance rule and the MML (05-50-00) as part of this investigation; any logbook entry required is the owner's, outside this document.
  • Hot-and-high plenum pressure (1744 mbar) exceeds the engine-deck value for those conditions (1711–1731) but is below the 1750 boost-control ceiling.

docs.title: 7. Resolution path (supersedes the diagnostic test plan)
docs.text:
Airmaster has identified the cause on their side and will update controller and hub firmware by remote session (website lists AC300 firmware 10_158, 9 Apr 2026, and hub DSD firmware 1_50, 28 Mar 2026; N117ZS has 10.139 / 1.43 from Nov 2025). Plan: 1. Remote session with Airmaster: diagnostics download (before), firmware update, parameter check. Record versions and any preset changes in the propeller logbook. 2. After the update: one normal takeoff in TO mode at KAWO on a cool day with AXIS logging; compare rpm/MAP amplitude and period against the Appendix A baseline on the same plot. Target: no sustained cycling. 3. If residual hunting remains ("teething problems"): send Airmaster the AXIS log and a controller diagnostics download for the same takeoff. 4. Interim operation until the update: Climb mode (5400) for routine takeoffs from long runways gives a steady ~100 kW (≈ 915iS takeoff power); TO mode where performance is needed. Not an engine-protection necessity on the data, but it removes the cycling.

The Hold/Manual discrimination flight (checklist rev 2) is retained in the project only as a record; it is no longer needed.

docs.title: 8. Open questions
docs.text:
• What the firmware changes (gain, deadband, rate) and what the remaining "teething problems" look like on other 916 installs — ask during the session.
  • Whether the TO preset stays at 5700 after the update.
  • Rotax Installation Manual: any governor response requirement or guidance on in-flight-adjustable props with the 916 boost schedule. Also the "CSA — Constant Speed Actuator" abbreviation in the OM suggests ECU provisions for a constant-speed system; ask Rotax what the ECU exposes.
  • Rotax ECU (BUDS) log of a takeoff: PCV duty cycle and TPS on the same timeline as rpm would close the boost-loop description.

docs.title: 9. References
docs.text:
• Rotax OM-916 i A/C24 Series, Ed0 Rev1 (Dec 2023): §2.1 operating limits (engine speed, manifold pressure, target pressures), §3.5 exceedance of operational limits, §7.6 air intake and boost pressure control, Ch. 5 engine deck.
  • Airmaster AP3/4/5 series Operator's Manual V5-1A (Hold and Manual mode operation, control loop description).
  • Airmaster SI-006 AC200 Operator Program Instructions R2b (operator-changeable flight variables; Hold RPM Max ≥ 100 rpm below engine max; A0117 cable). N117ZS has an AC300F — confirm the equivalent procedure with Airmaster.
  • N117ZS Airmaster Propeller Logbook, Leading Particulars (propeller) and Leading Particulars (controller), Rev1a.
  • Rotax SB-916i-003 / 915i-014 (overload clutch overspeed signature — ruled out).
  • Rotax-Owner.com thread 10523 (Airmaster governing band ±100 rpm; T/O preset 5700 practice).
  • Reproducible in SlingologyEIS Research (Spec 06): the Full-power segment preset over the flights dated through 2026-10-28 gives the Appendix A slice set; tests 7.1–7.4 give the swing, coupling, DA dependence and the two clean outliers. The app's period estimators give 3.8 s (IQR 3.5–4.1) where this write-up's peak count gave 4.4 s; see Spec 06 Q11.

docs.title: Appendix A — Every full-power segment, Apr–Oct 2026
Set up your aircraft and documents
docs.text: Ten minutes, once. What Claude should know about your aircraft before it investigates: how it is configured, what has been changed and when, and where your manuals are. All of it lives in Settings → Aircraft in the EIS pages, and Claude reads it at the start of every investigation.

docs.title: 1. The aircraft record
docs.text:
Open Settings → Aircraft. The aircraft was created with your first workspace and carries its engine model.

Fill in what you know: the airframe, the engine serial number, the propeller, the propeller controller, the firmware versions (one per line), the avionics. Save.

These are free text — write them as you would to a mechanic. Claude uses them to know which manual applies and which part a pattern might involve.

docs.title: 2. Notes: what changed, and when
docs.text:
Under Notes, keep a dated line for each change that might show in the engine data:

2026-03-02 — Propeller re-pitched at annual (+0.5°)
2026-06-18 — Controller firmware 2.14 → 2.16
2026-09-05 — Fuel pump replaced under SB-xx

Save notes. A pattern that starts on the day of a change is a different finding from one that has always been there; with these notes Claude can tell them apart and the Before / after prompt has something to compare.

docs.title: 3. Documents folders
docs.text:
On your computer, keep your copies of the Operators Manual, the service bulletins and the propeller and controller manuals in a folder (PDF, Markdown or text; subfolders are fine). Under Documents folders, type the folder's full path — e.g. /Users/you/Aircraft/Manuals — Add, then Save folders.

EIS reads them in place: nothing is copied into EIS, and nothing leaves your computer. Claude lists them, searches them for a phrase and reads the pages it needs, citing the page in the notebook. A changed file is re-read the next time it is used.

On the website this section is greyed and marked EXTENSION ONLY: a browser can't read a folder by its path. It works with the extension, or EIS installed with pip.

docs.title: 4. More than one workspace
docs.text:
This aircraft's workspaces lists every workspace of the aircraft. If a workspace is really another aircraft's — a test cell, a friend's logs, a different engine — the list says so when its engine differs from the record's:

This workspace's profile is Rotax 915 iS; the aircraft record says Rotax 916 iS. If it is another aircraft, move it to its own.

Move to another aircraft…, then pick the aircraft or A new aircraft… with a name, and Move. Claude opens the aircraft named in the extension's settings (or the only one), so keeping each aircraft's workspaces together keeps its investigations on the right flights.

docs.title: 5. Inbox sensitivity
docs.text:
Settings → Research sets how much the inbox raises for this workspace — quiet, normal or curious — with what each means in recent slices.

Start with normal. If the inbox raises things you keep marking Nothing here, try quiet; if you'd rather see more and dismiss more, curious.

docs.title: Export and import
docs.text: Five minutes. How to hand your whole workspace — flights, decisions and all — to another pilot, your mechanic, or anyone helping you read your engine; and how to open one someone sent you. The same export is your backup: the workspace lives in your browser's storage, and an export is the only copy that survives the site's data being cleared. Make one after each batch of decisions.

docs.title: 1. Decide what to share
docs.text:
Open Settings → App → Share a workspace. Two choices:

  • Include logs — on by default. The logs are what the recipient's app analyses; without them they get a description of a workspace but nothing to look at. Leave this on unless the recipient already has the logs.
  • Anonymise logs — off by default. Replaces your tail number and avionics ID with a pseudonym, blanks the GPS track and radio columns, and renames the files. Dates, times and engine hours stay, because the analysis needs them. The notice under the checkboxes says exactly this, every time.

The export is always the whole active workspace. To share only some flights, make a workspace that points at a folder containing just those logs, and export that.

Settings → App: include logs, anonymise, export, import.

docs.title: 2. Check your own words
docs.text: If you chose to anonymise, the export dialog lists the places where your tail number still appears in text you typed — notes, filter reasons, the workspace name. The app does not rewrite your words; edit them first if it matters.

docs.title: 3. Export
docs.text: Export workspace… writes one file: a .zip when logs are included, a small .eisworkspace file when not. Send it however you like. It contains your settings, every decision in force (filters, rule edits, exclusions, pins), your Journal and annotations, and the list of your flights — not the analysis results, which the recipient's app recomputes, and nothing about your computer or folder paths.

docs.title: 1. Open the file
docs.text: Settings → App → Import workspace…, or Import workspace… from the workspace switcher in the top bar. Import always creates a new workspace; it never changes one you have.

docs.title: 2. Read the summary
docs.text: Before anything is created, the app shows what is in the file: whose it is, which engine and app version, how many flights, how many filters and rule edits. The new workspace's name defaults to the sender's with (imported) added. If the file came from a newer version of the app than yours, the import is refused with a message; from an older one it proceeds with a notice.

docs.title: 3. Let it match the logs
docs.text:
The logs are unpacked into a folder of their own and matched against the sender's flight list:

38 of 40 flights found · 2 missing · 12 other logs held out

Then the usual analysis runs. You see the workspace as the sender saw it — their filters, exclusions and pins in force, their Journal entries, their annotations.

docs.title: 4. Understand the leftovers
docs.text:
• A flight the sender had but whose log did not arrive is listed under Skipped as In the sender's workspace — log not found. The sender's decisions about it wait until the log appears.
  • A log that was in the zip but not in the sender's workspace — perhaps they had skipped it — is held out, listed with Include if you want it.

docs.title: A note on what you are sharing
docs.text: An engine log carries your tail number, your avionics' serial number, the date and time of every flight and your GPS track. Anonymising removes the identity and the track. The dates remain. If that is more than you want to share, share fewer flights. See Sharing a workspace.

docs.title: Reading your first flight
docs.text: Five minutes. Open any flight from the Flights page — a longer one with a proper cruise is the most informative.

docs.title: The header: facts, not judgements
docs.text:
The top line is the date, duration, engine hours and the airport the log was named after. Beneath it, Flight facts: fuel burned, cruise miles per gallon, cruise fuel flow, and whether the lane check covered both lanes. These are logbook numbers for your planning. They are never compared with anything and never raise an alert, because wind, weight and the power you chose dominate them.

Contributes to reference means this flight is part of what the app considers normal for your engine.

Header with flight facts, this flight's insights, and the timeline with its phases.

docs.title: The left column: what needs your attention
docs.text:
Insights lists anything the app found worth saying about this flight. A LIMIT badge means an Operators Manual limit was crossed; the line under it says which, how far and for how long. A WATCH badge means a reading was unusual for your engine, or a trend has become clear. If the column is empty, nothing was flagged — the flight was ordinary.

Each insight offers the next step: View evidence jumps the chart to the moment; Filter this limit… and Edit trigger are decisions, covered in the next walkthrough.

docs.title: The timeline: the flight as the engine saw it
docs.text:
The chart plots a handful of channels — the Overview preset shows RPM, airspeed, oil temperature and EGT spread — each scaled to its own range so that shapes line up. Real values with units appear at the cursor. The coloured bands behind the traces are the phases of flight, and the caption below lists how long each lasted. Switch presets (Cylinders, Thermal, Power, Fuel system, Electrical) or add a channel to see something else; zoom with − and +. Across a whole flight each point on the chart summarises several seconds; zoom in to ten minutes or less and the chart redraws that stretch from every reading in the log, so the value at the cursor is the value the engine reported at that second.

Phases as coloured bands; durations in the caption.

docs.title: The Events table: limits and alerts
docs.text:
Below the chart, every Operators Manual limit crossed on this flight, and every unexpected engine-computer alert, as one row each: the time, the phase, which limit, how long, by how much. Chart jumps to the moment. A row is a fact about the flight; what to do about it is yours to decide.

Two marks on the chart go with a limit event. The triangle is where it started — the first reading past the limit, the row's Time — so the reading there is close to the limit itself. The value the row reports, worst 49.0 psi, is the furthest the reading went during the event, which on a long event can be minutes later; selecting the event draws a dashed line at that moment, labelled with the value. An engine-computer alert has no value, so it has no worst line.

A fuel-pressure event selected: it starts at the triangle and reaches its worst, 49.3 psi, at the dashed line.

Two limits exceeded on this flight, listed with duration and excess.

docs.title: The Analysis section: one card per topic
docs.text:
Each topic the app watches has a card. Most are collapsed to one line — this flight's number, your usual, the manual's limit:

Oil temperature peak · Peak 206°F. Your average: 200°F ± 12°F (49 flights). OM limit: 248°F.

Read across the line and you have the whole picture for that topic. A card expands only when it has something to add. The ? on each card explains what the topic measures and what a change can point to.

Cards with nothing to add stay on one line.

docs.title: Two notes you will see early on
docs.text:
Still building your reference — N more flights means there is not yet enough history to compare against; the number is shown, the judgement is withheld.

Not yet validated on this engine appears on a 915iS or 912iS: the topic works, but no data from such an engine has yet confirmed it behaves sensibly there.

docs.title: Reading habit
docs.text:
One unusual flight is a note to yourself. The same thing unusual on several flights is a pattern, and the place to see patterns is Trends, which is what the concept pages Your reference and Trends are about.

Next: From an insight to a decision.

docs.title: Your first investigation
docs.text: Twenty minutes. Ask Claude a question about your engine, watch it work through EIS, and read the notebook it writes. You need the extension installed and a workspace with your flights; your aircraft and documents set up make the answer better.

docs.title: 1. Pick a question
docs.text:
Something you noticed, in your own words. Good first questions name a flight and a feeling:

  • The climb after the touch-and-go at Bellingham on Oct 24 felt like a surge. Look into it.
  • Is there an oscillation during takeoff and initial climb?
  • Has the oil temperature in cruise changed since the new propeller?

Or start from the inbox, below the notebooks on the Research page: a pattern EIS raised is a question EIS noticed for you. Click its line to open it, then Show the evidence.

docs.title: 2. Ask
docs.text:
In Claude Desktop, open a new chat. Either type the question, or pick Investigate from the chat's + menu and give it the question — the prompt puts the EIS method in front of Claude: one flight first, then all of them; the manuals; a hypothesis with the alternatives ruled out; what it means and what to do.

For an inbox candidate, pick Look at this inbox item and give it the candidate's id (Claude can list them: what's in my EIS inbox?).

docs.title: 3. Watch it work — and steer
docs.text:
Claude says what it is doing as it goes: which flight it found and why, the window it is looking at, the slices it cut across your flights, the numbers that came back, the manual page it read. Steer as you would with a colleague:

Compare that with every other takeoff. Does it depend on density altitude? What does the controller manual say about its governing band?

Open Research in the EIS pages (http://127.0.0.1:8420/): the notebook is the first card, marked open, and fills in as Claude appends cells.

docs.title: 4. Read the notebook
docs.text:
Click its card on Research. When Claude finishes, the card carries the channels, flights, evidence and tests the notebook used, and two or three topic words Claude chose — click one to see every notebook about the same thing.

  • The header: the title, the card's marks and topic words, who wrote it, finished or still open, the engine version, the date, and whether its outputs are current for this workspace.
  • The answer first — a notebook is laid out in seven sections, and the first three are the part to read when you have five minutes: 1 The question, as you asked it, with its scope (the flights looked at, the manual pages used, what was taken as given, what the logs can't tell); 2 Answer — What the data shows, three to five sentences with their numbers, and What it means, a hypothesis with how sure Claude is and what would change it; 3 Proposed actions — each with who would do it and what it would settle, or None and why. If Claude came back to the notebook, the earlier answers are folded inside.

  • 4 Findings — each one a sentence and the table, figure or log view it rests on, numbered (Table 3) with a caption saying what it shows. A log view is the Flight view's chart for the window that matters, with Open flight to see it in the whole flight. The code is folded under show code, and a calculation behind a finding under show the calculation, for anyone who wants to check it.
  • 5 How this was done — the plan, the method, the alternatives Claude ruled out, and anything from outside your logs (a forum, another owner) labelled as context. 6 Follow-ups — dated, each ending with what changed above. 7 Working — the exploring Claude did on the way, folded.
  • Every number comes from a tool result, a code cell's output or a cited page; a mechanism is called a hypothesis. If something reads as a verdict without its reference, ask Claude where it came from.

docs.title: 5. Keep it, use it
docs.text:
• Re-run runs every code cell again on your current flights. Outputs that changed wait beside the old ones: Accept all new outputs or Discard all.
  • Everything else is under Actions. Export notebook (.zip) gives the notebook with its files, for another owner of the same engine — they import it from Research → Import a notebook…, and its cells re-run on their flights where they have EIS on their computer. Your logs don't travel.
  • Export as a page (.html) gives a page anyone can open — for a mechanic or a manufacturer's support desk, with two sentences of your own.
  • To keep the finding in the Journal, ask Claude when it finishes — put the finding in my Journal — and add what you decided there.

If the investigation came from the inbox, the item's line now opens to Open the investigation; mark it Watch, Acted (say what was done) or Nothing here from its ⋯ menu.

The original case, from a look at one flight to the notebook, is Reproducing a takeoff investigation.

docs.title: Open the app and your first workspace
docs.text: About fifteen minutes, most of it the app working. You need a computer with a current browser — the app is tested on macOS Chrome and Safari — and a folder of engine logs from your Garmin G3X or AXIS — the SD card's files, Garmin Pilot exports, or aircraft logs downloaded from flyGarmin. Nothing to install.

docs.title: 1. Open the app
docs.text:
Open SlingologyEIS in your browser. The first time, the page sets up the analysis engine — about 30 MB, downloaded once and kept by your browser — and shows its progress. Later visits take a few seconds, and work without a network: the app starts from the copy your browser kept. When a new version is published, the next visit with a network picks it up and says Updated to version … once.

Everything the app does from here on happens inside your browser, on your computer. Your logs are read from your own folders and never uploaded; the results are kept by your browser, on this device. There is no account and no server holding your data.

Prefer to run it yourself?

The same app can run as a small program on your own computer instead, with the workspace kept in an ordinary folder. See Running the app on your own computer at the end of this page. Everything else in this guide is the same either way.

docs.title: 2. Start a workspace — three ways
docs.text:
With no workspace yet, the app opens on Your first workspace: a name, the engine model, an optional tail number, and three ways to start, side by side. Name it after the aircraft. Choose the engine carefully — it decides which Operators Manual limits apply and cannot be changed later (you would make a new workspace).

The three ways to start. The same three appear under + New workspace later.
  • Load from a folder — the usual one. Choose folder… and pick the folder where you keep your logs; subfolders are included, and the app keeps reading it as you add more (step 3).
  • Create from logs — Create makes an empty workspace; then pick or drop log files onto the page.
  • Import a workspace — a workspace someone exported for you, or your own from another computer (Import workspace…). Its name comes with it.

The folder is a folder of logs, not another app's workspace.

docs.title: 3. Point it at your logs
docs.text:
No logs yet?

Skip this step and the next: download the sample workspace (10 MB) and use Settings → App → Import workspace… instead. It is a season of flights from the aircraft the app was developed on, decisions included. Pick up again at step 5 — the sample has four ground runs in Skipped, and the export and import walkthrough explains what an import does.

With Load from a folder, the folder you picked is already the workspace's. With Create from logs, click Choose folder… on the empty workspace and pick the folder where you keep your logs — subfolders are included — or drop files onto the page. The app only reads this folder; it never copies, moves or renames anything in it. You can add more folders later, and if you move logs around, Sync finds them again.

How the browser remembers the folder differs:

  • Chrome keeps the folder from one visit to the next. Now and then it asks you to confirm — the folder row shows Allow access; one click and you are back.
  • Safari does not keep folder access between visits. Your flights and analyses are all still there; the folder row says Not connected — reconnect, and you pick the folder again only when you want to sync new logs or open a flight's charts. The app says this once, on the row, the first time.

The app lists everything it found with Needs analysis beside each log, and an Analyze N button appears.

docs.title: 4. Analyze
docs.text:
Click Analyze. The app reads each log, decides whether it is a flight, works out the phases of flight, checks the Operators Manual limits and builds your reference. A season of logs takes a minute or two; the page shows progress per log. Leave the tab open until it finishes — the browser warns you if you try to close it mid-way.

When it finishes, a notice sums up what happened — on N117ZS's 124 logs, 61 new flights analyzed, three exact copies skipped, one aircraft log added to the flight its AXIS card log already made, and 59 files skipped — not a flight — and the list fills in.

The summary of the first analysis, then every flight with its date, duration, engine hours, insights and source.

This workspace lives in your browser

Clearing the site's data would remove it. Before you go further, see step 7, Keep a copy — an export takes a few seconds.

docs.title: 5. Look at what was skipped
docs.text:
Click Skipped. Logs that did not become flights are listed with the reason: a ground run, a flight under ten minutes, a log with a gap in it. This is normal — every engine start writes a log, and most of a year's logs are not flights. If one looks wrong, open it to check and click Include.

Skipped logs, each with its reason, each includable.

docs.title: 6. What to expect from the first flights
docs.text: Your reference needs about ten flights before it can say what is usual for your engine. Until then, cards show their numbers with still building instead of a comparison, and the Trends page says building reference. The Operators Manual checks work from the first flight.

docs.title: 7. Keep a copy
docs.text:
Your workspace lives in your browser's storage for this site. That survives closing the tab, restarting the browser and app updates — but it is gone if you clear the site's data, and a browser short of disk space — or Safari, after a long time without a visit — may clear it on its own. Settings → App → Storage shows how much space the app uses and whether the browser has agreed to keep it. Export workspace… on the same page writes a single file that restores everything; make one once your first analysis is done, and again after you have made decisions you would not want to redo. The export and import walkthrough has the details.

Next: Reading your first flight. To understand what just happened, Logs, flights and workspaces.

docs.title: Running the app on your own computer
docs.text:
The app can also run as a small program on your Mac, Windows or Linux computer, with the workspace kept in an ordinary folder (~/SlingologyEIS) rather than in the browser. Pilots choose this when they want the data in a folder they can back up like any other, when several browsers on one machine should share one workspace, or when they add log folders by typing a path. The screens, the analysis and the results are identical.

You need Python 3.10 or later. Download the latest slingology_eis…whl file from the project's releases page, then in a terminal:

pip install slingology_eis-<version>-py3-none-any.whl
slingology-eis serve

The last line prints an address — http://127.0.0.1:8420/ — open it in your browser. Leave the terminal window open while you use the app; Ctrl-C there stops it. Nothing listens on your network; the app is reachable only from this computer.

The differences you will notice: log folders are added by typing their path (or dropping files) and stay connected without any browser permissions; Settings → App shows Data location instead of Storage; and the workspace is in that folder, so the browser's site data does not matter. A workspace export from one way of running the app imports into the other.

docs.title: From an insight to a decision
docs.text: Ten minutes. This follows one real case: a fuel-pressure limit that is exceeded on most flights because of the installation, and what to do about it so it stops burying everything else.

docs.title: 1. Notice the pattern
docs.text:
On the Flights page, nearly every flight carries a LIMIT badge. Open one and the insight reads:

⚠ [CAUTION] Fuel pressure maximum: 3 events, worst 49.3 psi (max 46.0 psi), 11 min 36 s past the limit.

The insights column: a takeoff-RPM overshoot and a fuel-pressure excursion.

A limit crossed once is worth a look. A limit crossed on 50 of 61 flights by about the same margin is a characteristic of this aircraft, and the question becomes: do I understand it, and do I accept it? In this case the fuel-pressure sender reads a few psi high, confirmed against a gauge at the annual. That is a reason — and the app wants the reason written down.

docs.title: 2. Open the filter editor
docs.text:
Click Filter this limit… on the insight (or on the event's row in the Events table). The editor opens in place and starts by telling you what it knows:

On the 50 of your flights that went past this limit, it typically went 3.3 psi past, at most 4.6 psi.

The filter editor: magnitude, duration, phases, and the reason.

docs.title: 3. Choose what to tolerate
docs.text:
Three conditions, any one of which tolerates an event:

  • A little past the limit is fine, up to — the app suggests the worst you have seen, 4.6 psi, which with the 46 psi limit means readings up to 50.6 psi. Set it to what you actually accept.
  • Brief events are fine, lasting up to — leave unticked here; duration is not the issue.
  • Events in these phases are fine — leave unticked; this excursion happens in cruise, where it matters most.

Write the reason in Why is this fine on your aircraft? It appears in the Journal and in any export you share.

docs.title: 4. Preview, then apply
docs.text:
Click Preview. The app counts the effect across the whole workspace before anything changes:

This would hide 184 events on 50 of 61 flights; no flight would show a breach.

That last part is the check that the band is wide enough for the pattern you know, and no wider. Then Apply to all flights — and note the caption above it: All flights in this workspace — this limit. A filter is a statement about your aircraft, not about one flight.

docs.title: 5. What changes
docs.text:
On every Flight view, those fuel-pressure events collapse into one line — N events within your filter, up to +4.6 psi — expandable if you want them. The LIMIT badges those flights carried only for this reason disappear from the Flights page, and the insights that remain are the ones that are new.

The same flight afterwards: the fuel-pressure events are within your filter, labelled INFO.

What does not change: the Operators Manual limit still reads 46 psi, the events are still detected and still appear on the Trends page's Limit: fuel press max panel, and the app has frozen a reference of your twenty most recent flights with this event.

docs.title: 6. What the app keeps watching
docs.text:
Open the Journal. The filter is listed on one line under Limit filters, with what it hides now; Manage limit filters → opens its card with its status — Stable to begin with. From now on every new flight is compared with the frozen reference. If the sender starts reading five psi high instead of three, or events become more frequent, the status changes to Drifting; an event the band does not cover shows as a Breach; after 50 engine hours it asks for a Review. Each of these is counted on the Journal badge in the top bar and announced in a banner on the Flights page, so a filter never becomes a blind spot.

Journal → Manage limit filters: status, how far past the limit each flight went, time past the limit, and the frozen reference.

docs.title: The other decisions
docs.text:
The same shape — see the effect, state the scope, record it in the Journal — applies to the rest:

  • Edit trigger on an insight, or Edit rules… on any topic card, opens the rule editor beside the card. Change how many flights a comparison needs or how strong a trend must be; a live preview counts how many flights would gain or lose an insight; Apply to all flights.
  • Exclude this flight from reference on an insight, or the flight's header: give a reason and the flight stops shaping what others are compared against. This flight only.
  • Enable/disable a topic in the rule editor: the card stays on every flight, collapsed, with Enable.

All of them are explained on Your decisions. Next: Export and import.

docs.title: Install the extension
docs.text: Five minutes. How to add SlingologyEIS to Claude Desktop on a Mac, so Claude can investigate your engine logs on your computer. You need the Claude Desktop app, signed in with your own Claude account.

docs.title: 1. Download the file for your Mac
docs.text:
Open the latest release and download one file:

  • Apple silicon (M1, M2, M3, M4…): slingology-eis-…-macos-arm64.mcpb
  • Intel: slingology-eis-…-macos-x86_64.mcpb

Not sure which you have? Apple menu → About This Mac: a line Chip naming Apple M… is Apple silicon; a line Processor naming Intel is Intel.

The file is about 100 MB. It holds the EIS engine, its own copy of Python and the EIS pages; you don't need to install anything else.

docs.title: 2. Install it in Claude Desktop
docs.text:
With Claude Desktop open, do any one of these:

  • double-click the downloaded .mcpb file;
  • drag it onto the Claude Desktop window;
  • in Claude Desktop, Settings → Extensions → Advanced settings → Install Extension… and pick the file.

Claude Desktop opens its install view: SlingologyEIS, what it does and the tools it offers. Install it from there.

The file isn't signed yet. Claude Desktop warns you before installing an extension that isn't signed. If you downloaded it from the SlingologyEIS releases page above, install it anyway. Signing comes in a later release.

docs.title: 3. Settings — all optional
docs.text:
Claude Desktop shows the extension's settings during the install, and later under Settings → Extensions → SlingologyEIS. Each can be left empty:

Setting Leave empty to… Set it when… EIS data folder use the folder the EIS pages use (Settings → App → Data location) you keep EIS's data somewhere specific, e.g. on another disk Aircraft use your only aircraft, or the one you opened last you have more than one aircraft in EIS Log folders link folders later, from the EIS pages you want your log folders linked to the aircraft's workspace from the start

Log folders added here are added to the workspace Claude uses; removing one is done in the EIS pages.

docs.title: 4. First start
docs.text:
Open a new chat in Claude Desktop. The first time, EIS takes a few seconds longer to start (about ten) while it sets itself up; after that it starts at once.

While Claude Desktop is open, the EIS pages are at http://127.0.0.1:8420/ in your browser. Open them:

  • With no workspace yet, they show the first-workspace steps — the same as on the website (Open the app and your first workspace). Creating the workspace also creates the aircraft.
  • Been using the website? Keep Claude Desktop open, go back to the website and press Move my workspace to EIS on this computer — on Research, or in Settings → App. It sends your questions and marks, notes, journal and decisions (not the logs) and opens the EIS pages here with the workspace selected. Then, on Flights, add the folder that holds your logs and Sync: the flights are analysed here, and your marks open them. The website keeps its copy, marked this is now the copy; from now on you work at http://127.0.0.1:8420/. If EIS here already has a workspace, the moved one is added beside it — never merged.
  • If you already run EIS on your computer (slingology-eis serve), the pages are served by that one; the extension leaves it alone and Claude's tools still work.

docs.title: 5. Check that Claude sees EIS
docs.text:
In the chat, ask:

What does EIS have for my aircraft?

Claude calls EIS's guide and tells you the aircraft, the workspace it uses, how many flights, and anything waiting in the inbox. In the chat's + menu you'll find the four EIS prompts — Investigate, Look at this inbox item, Before / after, Review new flights (the prompts).

Next: Set up your aircraft and documents, then Your first investigation.

docs.title: If something is wrong
docs.text:
• Nothing happens when you open the file. Use Settings → Extensions → Advanced settings → Install Extension… instead, and make sure Claude Desktop is up to date.
  • Claude says no workspace yet. Open http://127.0.0.1:8420/ and create a workspace (step 4), then ask again.
  • The pages don't open. Something else is using port 8420, or Claude Desktop isn't running. Check Settings → Extensions: SlingologyEIS should be enabled.
  • Logs to send with a problem report: Claude Desktop's own, in ~/Library/Logs/Claude/, and EIS's, cache/mcp.log inside your EIS data folder.

To turn the extension off or remove it, open it under Settings → Extensions. Your workspaces and logs stay where they are.

docs.title: Mark something for Claude
docs.text: Five minutes. Find something odd on a flight, mark it with a sentence under a question, and hand the question to Claude. Marking works on the website and on your computer; handing it to Claude needs the extension installed.

docs.title: 1. Open the flight and turn on Signal
docs.text: Open the flight on Flights. Under the chart, press Signal. Under each channel a strip shows how far it swings, second by second, and below it where it repeats — lit where a period stands out, with the period in the line above (RPM — swing, and where it repeats (≈ 3.8 s, lit 10 % of the flight)).

docs.title: 2. Zoom to what looks odd
docs.text: Drag across the chart to the stretch you mean. With Signal on, its numbers appear under the chart: the swing beside the Operators Manual line it approaches, the period, and how the other channels move with the first.

docs.title: 3. Mark for Claude
docs.text:
Press Mark for Claude… beside Signal. Write what you see, in your words — rpm wanders by about 100 at full power, MAP with it. Then choose the question it belongs to:

  • an open question — the newest is chosen; marks of the same thing on other flights belong together;
  • a new question — give it a short title (rough climbs);
  • none for now — it waits under Unassigned.

Press Mark. The line beside the button says where it went: Marked 10:16–11:02 under “rough climbs” (1 mark) in Research → Inbox.

docs.title: 4. Mark it again, elsewhere
docs.text: If you have seen it on other flights, mark those windows under the same question. Two or three marks tell Claude more than one.

docs.title: 5. Find it in the inbox
docs.text: Research in the top bar: your question is in the inbox below the notebooks — click its line to see its marks. A mark opens its flight at the window, with the channels you were looking at. The ⋯ menus rename the question, edit a note, move a mark to another question, or delete one.

docs.title: 6. Hand it to Claude
docs.text:
In Claude Desktop, open a new chat, press +, choose Investigate, and send it with no text: Claude takes your newest open question, opens a notebook with your marks — your note, then a log view of each window — and starts from what you saw. To pick another question, type its title. The question shows investigating in the inbox, and Open the investigation takes you to the notebook (Your first investigation).

On the website, the inbox says the question is waiting for Claude and how to install the extension.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Investigations — what Claude does with a question.
  • What EIS measures — what the Signal strips and numbers are.

docs.title: Run a notebook in JupyterLab
docs.text: Fifteen minutes the first time. An investigation is an ordinary Jupyter notebook: you can open it in JupyterLab, run it top to bottom against your own workspace, change it, and save it — and the Research page shows what you ran. For readers who know Python; nothing here is needed to read a notebook.

docs.title: 1. Install JupyterLab with EIS
docs.text:
JupyterLab needs EIS installed in its own Python. In Terminal, with Python 3.10 or newer, and the slingology_eis-….whl file from the latest release in your Downloads folder:

python3 -m venv ~/eis-jupyter
~/eis-jupyter/bin/pip install "$(ls ~/Downloads/slingology_eis-*.whl | tail -1)[investigations]" jupyterlab ipykernel
~/eis-jupyter/bin/python -m ipykernel install --user --name slingology-eis --display-name "SlingologyEIS"

The last line registers a kernel called SlingologyEIS. It reads the same EIS data folder as the pages and the extension, so it sees the same workspaces.

docs.title: 2. Find the notebook's file
docs.text:
A notebook lives in your EIS data folder:

<data folder>/workspaces/<workspace id>/studies/<study id>/notebook.ipynb
  • Data folder: EIS pages → Settings → App → Data location.
  • Workspace id: on the notebook's page, open the first show code (setup: binds eis to this workspace) — it reads eis.open("ws_…").
  • Study id: the end of the page's address, #/research/st-….

Or work on a copy: Export notebook (.zip), unzip it, and open notebook.ipynb from there (your changes then stay in the copy).

docs.title: 3. Run it
docs.text:
~/eis-jupyter/bin/jupyter lab

Open notebook.ipynb, choose the SlingologyEIS kernel, and Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells. The setup cell binds eis to the workspace; every later cell uses it — eis.flights(), eis.cycling("full_power", "rpm"), eis.logview(...) (the eis library). Log views show as pictures in JupyterLab; the EIS pages show them as live charts.

Nothing is fenced in JupyterLab: the kernel is yours, with your permissions, unlike the bench Claude's code runs on.

docs.title: 4. Save it, and see it in EIS
docs.text:
Saving in place (⌘S) updates the notebook EIS holds — it is that file. On the Research page the cells you ran are marked ran elsewhere, and the header counts them. Then either:

  • Keep outputs that ran elsewhere — accept them as they are; or
  • Re-run — EIS runs the cells again on its own bench, and you accept or discard what changed.

If you saved a copy instead, import it from Research → Import a notebook…: it arrives as a new notebook.

docs.title: Sharing a notebook
docs.text: Ten minutes, two people. How to send another owner of the same engine the notebook that found something on your aircraft, and how they run it on theirs — without either of you sending a single flight log. Also how to send it to someone with no EIS at all. To follow along alone, make a second workspace pointing at a different folder of logs and play both parts.

docs.title: What a notebook carries, and what it doesn't
docs.text: The exported notebook holds the question, Claude's narrative, the code and every output — numbers, tables, figures, the pictures of its log views — and any files Claude wrote. It names your flights by fingerprint: a code derived from each log that means nothing to anyone who does not hold the same file. Your logs do not travel, and the recipient's never have to.

docs.title: 1. Read it as they will
docs.text: Open the notebook on the Research page and choose Actions → Export as a page (.html). Open the page in your browser: that is everything the recipient will read. If a note or a cell names a person or a place you'd rather not send, ask Claude to change it.

docs.title: 2. Export
docs.text:
• For another EIS owner: Export notebook (.zip).
  • For a mechanic, a manufacturer or a forum: the .html page from step 1 — it opens in any browser.

Send it however you like, with a line saying what you found and what you'd like them to look at.

docs.title: 3. Import
docs.text: On your Research page, Import a notebook… and pick the .zip (or a bare .ipynb). EIS matches the notebook's flights against your workspace and opens it.

docs.title: 4. Read it — as theirs
docs.text: If none of the sender's flights are in your workspace (the usual case between two aircraft), each log view shows the sender's saved picture and every output is the sender's; the line under the title says the outputs are read-only and not about this workspace.

docs.title: 5. Run this on my flights
docs.text:
With EIS on your computer, press Run this on my flights. EIS copies the notebook as a new one — … — my flights — and runs every code cell against your own flights. Now the measurements are about your aircraft: put its count and swing beside the sender's, and you see at once whether you share the behaviour.

A cell that named one of the sender's flights has no flight to load here; ask Claude to point it at the matching flight of yours ("the first takeoff on my last flight").

docs.title: 6. Keep both
docs.text: The imported notebook stays in your list as the sender's record; your run is a second notebook.

docs.title: If some flights do match
docs.text: If the sender also gave you their logs (a shared workspace, say), cells whose flights you hold are live, and the rest show the sender's outputs.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Notebooks you keep and share — what a notebook is.
  • From a finding to action — writing to a manufacturer with two aircraft's evidence.

docs.title: Reproducing a takeoff investigation
docs.text: Twenty minutes. This repeats, with EIS and Claude, the investigation that found a 180-rpm, four-second cycle on nearly every takeoff of one aircraft — a behaviour that lived inside every limit and never changed, so neither the Flight view's events nor Trends could have shown it. Any workspace with a season of flights will do; the numbers below are the original aircraft's (60 flights, April to October). The original write-up is here. You need the extension installed for steps 4–6.

docs.title: What you will do
docs.text: Look at one flight with Signal on, mark the takeoffs that look odd, ask Claude with Investigate, and read the notebook it writes.

docs.title: 1. Look at the flight it was felt on
docs.text:
Open the three-takeoff AXIS flight of 2026-10-24 (§2.3 of the write-up) — Flights, or Find a flight with Oct 24 three landings. Choose rpm and manifold pressure on the chart, and press Signal under it.

The swing strip under rpm brightens over the three full-power segments and stays dim through taxi and cruise; the repeat strip lights over the same three stretches, and the line above it reads a period of three to four seconds. Something repeats at takeoff power, and only there.

docs.title: 2. Read one takeoff's numbers
docs.text: Drag across the first takeoff. Under the chart: rpm swings about 170 rpm peak to peak, beside the Operators Manual's takeoff-rpm line it approaches; it repeats every three to four seconds; and manifold pressure moves with it, correlation high at zero lag. Two signals in step is a mechanism, not a wobble — but this is one takeoff on one flight.

docs.title: 3. Mark it — and the others
docs.text:
Press Mark for Claude…, write rpm and MAP swing together at full power, choose A new question and call it takeoff rpm oscillation. Mark.

Zoom to the second and third takeoffs and mark each under the same question (it is offered first). If you remember another flight where it felt the same, mark that too. Research shows the question in the inbox with its marks (Mark something for Claude).

docs.title: 4. Ask
docs.text:
In Claude Desktop, open a new chat, choose Investigate from +, and send it with no text. Claude takes takeoff rpm oscillation, opens a notebook with your three marks — your note, then a log view of each takeoff — and starts from what you saw. In the chat you will see it:

  • read your aircraft notes and find the flight;
  • cut every full-power segment of every flight — on the original aircraft, 98 slices from 59 of 60 flights (touch-and-go sessions give several each);
  • ask whether rpm cycles across them — in 93 of 98 slices, every 3.8 s, swing 180 rpm;
  • ask whether manifold pressure and fuel flow move with it — MAP in step, fuel flow a second behind;
  • read the boost schedule in your Operators Manual, and the governor's band in the controller manual if it is in your documents folders;
  • test the hypothesis against density altitude — the swing fades at high density altitude, where the boost control has reached its ceiling.

Each of those is a cell in the notebook, with its output.

docs.title: 5. Steer
docs.text: Ask what you would ask a colleague. "Is it the same on G3X and AXIS logs?" — Claude will say the G3X damps manifold pressure, so the coupling shows weaker there. "Which takeoffs don't cycle?" — the two clean ones were high-altitude departures. "What does the controller manual say about its governing band?"

docs.title: 6. Read the notebook
docs.text:
On the Research page the notebook opens with the question and Claude's summary: what was found, with counts and references; the mechanism, stated as a hypothesis; the alternatives ruled out, each with the cell that did it; and what to do. Your question in the inbox now reads watching, with Open the investigation.

  • Ask Claude to note the finding in the Journal, so the date is kept.
  • Export as a page (.html) for the person who can act on it (From a finding to action).
  • Export notebook (.zip) for another owner of the same engine (Sharing a notebook).

docs.title: What happened next
docs.text: The owner sent the plot and the per-takeoff table to the propeller controller's manufacturer, who recognised a known behaviour of that controller with this engine and offered a firmware update. Once the update is flown, the Before / after prompt with its date compares the takeoffs on each side.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Investigations — what Claude does, and what stays true.
  • What EIS measures — the slices and tests behind the numbers.
